speechtext:
Bail was not provided by the Department of Justice, neither was any person directed to provide bail when the defendants were arrested in the first instance. The men concerned arranged the bonds required between themselves and members of the force. During the hearing of the commission proceedings, however, Agent Eccles was arrested on a charge of perjury during the Victoria proceedings and bail set at $3,000. considered Eccles should be protected and the Department of Justice instructed that so long as Eccles enjoyed the confidence of his superiors, the government should protect him to the extent of furnishing the necessary bail. The officer commanding the mounted police in Vancouver, therefore, instructed Inspector Shoebotham to arrange bail for Eccles in this particular case only. Sureties of $1,500 each were accepted from Inspector Shoebotham and Mr. M. C. Hill, of Vancouver.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, good faith should be kept with the Maritime provinces and other interested parts of the Dominion in regard to the recorded assurances and undertakings of governments and parliament and the agreements set out in the statutes of the Dominion respecting the routing of Canadian trade over Canadian territory and through Canadian ports, and, that freight rates over the Intercolonial railway be adjusted in accordance with the understanding of confederation.
He said:	In moving this resolution I do
not desire to weary the House by repeating what I have said in former sessions. At the same time there are a large number of new members in this parliament who are not familiar, perhaps, with the history of confederation as established in 1867, with the statements of leading public men before and since confederation, or with the agreements and enactments of parliament dealing with the Maritime provinces. This resolution takes us back to the representations of the Fathers of Confederation made to the Maritime provinces, also to the assurances and pledges of representative men, and to parliamentary enactments and agreements extending back for the past fifty years or more. In confirmation of that statement let me quote first from the speeches of Fathers of Confederation. The following are the words of the Hon. Geo. Brown, spoken at Halifax on September 12, 1864:
But far in advance of all other advantages would be this: That union of all the provinces would break down all trade barriers between us and throw open at once to all a combined market of four millions of people. You in the east would send us your fish
2308	COMMONS
Maritime Rights-Mr. Black (Halifax)
and your coals and your West India produce, while we would send you in return the flour and the grain and the meats you now buy in Boston and New York.
Sir George Etienne Cartier said at a banquet at Halifax on the same date, September 12, 1864:
Canada has population and territory sufficient to make a great nation in course of time. But she wants what the lower provinces possess, an outlet to the sea. As the lower provinces now stand they are comparatively weak and powerless, and the wealth, labour and industry which Canada possesses go in a great measure to enrich such cities as New York, Boston and Portland. This must continue to be the case until the Intercolonial railway, of which we have ever been an advocate, shall be built, and as soon as the colonies are confederated the .construction of that work will undoubtedly commence.
Again at a later date in Montreal, October 23, he is reported as saying:
I must repeat to you what I stated while in the lower provinces, that while we possessed the personal and the territorial elements which go to constitute a nation, we were wanting in the maritime element. During six months of the year we had to knock at the door of our neighbour in order to carry on our trade. This cannot be tolerated. This confederation must be carried out. With our prosperity we are enriching the American states, whereas we ought to be enriching our own states. We ought to be enriching such harbours as St. John and Halifax.
Sir Jo'hn A. Macdonald was not silent. On the same occasion he said:
I don't hesitate to say that with respect to the Intercolonial railway it is understood by the people of Canada-
That is Ontario and Quebec; they were oalled Canada at that time, I believe.
-that it can only be built as a means of political union for the colonies. It cannot be denied that the railway, as a commercial enterprise, would be of comparatively little commercial advantage to the people of Canada. Whilst we have the St. Lawrence in summer and the America ports in time of peace, we have all that is requisite for our purposes. We recognize, however, the fact that peace may not always exist and that we must have some other means of outlet if we do not wish to be cut off from the ocean for some months in the year. We wish to feel greater security-to know that we can have assistance readily in the hour of danger. In the case of a union this railway must be a national work, and Canada will cheerfully contribute.
These leaders of thought in the political arena must have realized that the trade of the Maritimes, then closely identified with the markets of New York, other large American cities and the New England states, would be transferred almost wholly to the markets of western Canada, and with this in view they provided the means of transportation, namely the Intercolonial railway.
My first visit to the west was by steamer from Halifax to Portland; thence by the Grand Trunk railway to Montreal. The building of the Intercolonial was intended to change

this. It may be said that the Intercolonial was built and the intended terms of confederation fulfilled. My answer to that is: The line was built and its rightful terminus should be the city of Montreal. It has been chopped off at Riviere du Loup. It is maimed and a profitable section is thrown into the region known as the central. The Intercolonial railway has lost its identity in the National Railway system, and is subjected to prohibitive freight rates, and has therefore ceased to be a developer of trade from the Maritimes to the central provinces. The Intercolonial railway was to be a national highway westwardly for the Maritime provinces. It is prevented from performing its national mission. The way is blocked by prohibitive freight rates. The building of the Intercolonial is in vain, if its primary and vital purposes be defeated. They are defeated as I have stated. Would there be anything unreasonable in asking that the Intercolonial be operated on the same basis as the canals of Ontario and Quebec.
Now, Mr. Speaker, passing over the utterances of many other public men, I come to the time when the building by the government of the day of a transcontinental railway was before parliament. The Maritimes were even then not forgotten. They were promised direct benefit from this proposal. What was that advantage to be? Listen to what the Hon. W. S. Fielding said in this House in 1903, That gentleman was a representative of the province of Nova Scotia in the government of that day. He said:
With this road built, instead of being dependent on the Canadian Pacific railway only, St. John will have two strings to its bow. Not a pound of traffic that goes to St. John now will be taken away, and St. John will stand its chance of getting a fair share of the new traffic to be created by this road. Halifax with its peerless harbour will have advantages which it has not hitherto enjoyed. Surely, Sir, the time has come after years of deception, humbugging and trickery about the lines to the Maritime provinces, that faith should be kept with these people, and they should have a through line running on Canadian territory from ocean to ocean.
On the same occasion, July 30, 1903, what did Sir Wilfrid Laurier say? The then leader of the government used these words:
Now, Sir, we lay it down as a principle, on which we are to be judged by friend and foe, that we are to have a transcontinental railway, and that its terminus must be in Canadian waters, and that the whole line, every inch of it, must be in Canadian territory. We say further, that such a line i3 a necessity to our commercial independence.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier said further:
Now, there is another feature of this contract to which I shall call the attention of the House. If we have gone into this contract, our intention has been, as stated in the preamble to force traffic in Cana-

Maritime Rights-Mr. Black (Halifax)
dian channels and through Canadian waters. We have made it a special condition of the contract and this condition is expressed in section 42, as follows:
"It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railways, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ports."
This principle is further emphasized by the paragraph following, No. 43, which says:
The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those provided above, but shall in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely the development of trade through Canadian ocean ports and Canadian channels.
What has been done by governments during the past twenty-two years to carry out these enactments of parliament, or to keep faith in regard to the contracts entered into by government and ratified by parliament? The situation in the Maritimes gives the answer.
The foregoing contracts were made in 1903. We come to the year 1911. What happened then? The Canadian Northern Ontario Railway, which was part of the Mackenzie and Mann project, sought assistance from the government, and this aid was given under the following condition-I quote from a clause in the agreement:
It is hereby declared that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government for the express purpose of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
In the year 1914 further aid to the extent of 145,000.000 was granted and the principle laid down in the contracts of 1903 and 1911 was reaffirmed in most unmistakable and emphatic language.
There can be no question about the meaning of the clauses in the contracts which I have quoted, nor does any other clause throw doubt on their meaning. What has been done to carry out its terms? The late Senator Fowler, in 1904, while he was a member of the House of Commons, moved an amendment to strengthen the contract of 1903 in the interest of the Maritimes. This amendment Mr. Fielding on behalf of the government refused to accept and in refusing, he used these words:
The government said that they would put in words that would serve the purpose better, and they would
put them, not in the charter, but in the contract, and that would bind the company to these terms. So we put in the contract the section which has been printed in the press, declaring in explicit terms that the company accepts the aid given them by the government on the condition that it is the object and purpose to promote trade through Canadian channels and through Canadian ports.
What further did the Hon. Mr. Fielding say? His words were that the government of the day intended to build the Transcontinental railway so that the products of western Canada would without fail flow uninterruptedly over an all-Canadian line to the ports of Halifax and St. John. Has this materialized? Has anything been done to carry out these pledges? The Hon. R. W. Scott, leader of the government in the Senate, when speaking on the question on October 12, 1903, used these words:
Therefore, it is to our interest if we are going to develop our Maritime ports, if we are going to have that grain go east through Halifax and ports along the St. Lawrence, to do something In order to induce it to go there.
This is a clipping from, I think, the Montreal Gazette, or at least one of the Montreal papers of the other day. Premier Tasehereau said:
I believe every Canadian, whether he be in British Columbia, or Quebec, or Ontario, should join with the Maritime provinces to give them what is necessary for them to live and thrive. They need cheap transportation. That perhaps was not the letter of the confederation pact, but it certainly was the spirit when the Intercolonial railway was built. Speaking as a Canadian, as a citizen of the province of Quebec, I have no hesitation in saying that it is the duty of those who govern Canada to-day to see that this important part of Canada (the Maritimes) is looked after and is satisfied.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House discussing the figures showing Nova Scotia's contribution to national railways and canals, nor do I touch upon the burden borne by Nova Scotia in providing railways and canals, none of which touches Nova Scotia. These are the pledges of the government confirmed and enacted by parliament, providing a national policy which was to have been carried out, but which, unfortunately for the Maritimes, has not been put into force. The national railway policy is defined, the government has its instructions from parliament, and not only should know what to do, but should do it. It should put the policy, so unmistakably defined, into operation and not attempt to side-track the issue by reference of the Maritime situation to a royal commission, as is suggested in the Speech from the Throne. We of the Maritimes protest most strongly and emphatically against any action by this government, such
2310	COMMONS
Maritime Rights-Mr. Black (Halifax)
as reference to a royal commission or otherwise, that will have a tendency to delay the full consideration and equitable readjustment of the Martimes' just claims beyond the present session of parliament. We shall be ready at all times to co-operate in any investigation that may be held with the bona fide intention of discovering or elaborating these injustices, 'but we insist that prompt and definite action must be taken at the present session and that a declaration of policy in regard to these matters be made by the government indicating that the government is prepared to give belated justice to the Maritime provinces. It is the duty of the government to assume the responsibility and to deal with the problem themselves at this session of parliament. Only a few days ago a minister of the crown said:
I have always considered that the people's wishes could best be expressed by the voice of their representatives in parliament.
Those are the words of the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) in March last as reported on page 1600 of Hansard. The representatives of the Maritime provinces are expressing the wishes of our people and we unanimously demand that they be carried out.
I have some interesting statements to reveal to the House in connection with the Martime situation as it relates to the Intercolonial railway. In 1021 the Halifax Herald, one of the most enterprising papers in the Dominion of Canada, asked this question of all candidates nominated for election in December of that year:
Realizing importance of campaign which our newspaper has consistently supported for restoration of Maritime rights with C.N.R. by establishment of eastern unit, with headquarters at Moncton in charge of Maritime trained men, we would apprecite if you would favour us with a brief, definite statement of your attitude on the question.
This is the answer of the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald):	I
quote only his answer and that of the representative of Prince county, P.E.I. (Mr. MacLean), they being members of this House representing Maritime province constituencies. The Minister of National Defence replied:
For the past year and a half I have consistently urged that the only method to enable the industries of the Maritime provinces to be carried on with any degree of success would be by detaching the Intercolonial altogether from the C.N.R. and G.T.R. connections, and running and operating it as it was operated for forty years under the terms of confederation. We would thus be freed from the taxation which is now imposed upon the patrons of the road for the purpose of paying the interest upon the enormous debts contracted by the C.N.R. in its construction in western Canada. The control of the

Intercolonial must be taken from Toronto and vested in Moncton, where it always was, and the railway should be officered by men in sympathy with Maritime interests and Maritime rights.
The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) said:
I have advocated on every platform during the campaign that the Maritime provinces should, under the terms of confederation, have special consideration and special treatment; that the railroad was given, not as a dividend earning road but that our products should be transported to the markets of the world at a reasonable rate, and any deficits on the road should be cheerfully born by the federal government. I have made strong plea for the establishment of an eastern unit with office at Moncton, with a practical man in charge who understands conditions, and that freights should not favour western Canada as at present, as we pay the same rate to St. John and Sydney as Montreal pays. They call it the people's railroad but over here we are taxed for it.
What, may I ask, has the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Macdonald) done to carry out his ideas as expressed in his message to the Halifax Herald? Surely he did not hesitate for lack of support, backed as he was by every member from Nova Scotia, sixteen in number. He has not had to wait for demands from that province that good faith be kept. Has he made representation to the government of the requirements of his province, and been over-ruled by his colleagues? What has he, the representative in the government of Nova Scotia, done?
His utterances and his promises have fallen to the winds. He could not go back to his own native constituency, but sought another where he was not so well known.
Our Maritime members are not here to sit silent and inactive as regards our provinces, as was the case during the last parliament; we are making our demands and will press them to the utmost.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to set forth some of the matters to which we call the earnest attention of this government. I ask them to drop commissions and, so to speak, get down to business. Parliament has given them instructions; we ask the government to obey the instructions. I might summarize some of the matters which I feel sure are in the minds of the people of the Maritime provinces, in respect to which they believe they have grievances and for the redress of which grievances they feel that there should be practical action on the part of the government and parliament. Before doing so I may say that underlying the slumbering dissatisfaction which has existed in those provinces for a long time, and which was marked by the ballot box demonstrations of the people in June and October of last year, there is the growing conviction that the Maritimes have been

Maritime Rights-Mr. MacLaren
treated by governments and parliaments as minor and unimportant partners in confederation, whom it was safe to neglect, whose interests might be sidetracked, and whose requests for fair play might be postponed.
The election results to which I referred a moment ago clearly show that the patience of the Maritime people is exhausted; that they are now standing for their rights within the Dominion as full partners of the confederation, and that they will not be turned aside nor satisfied by empty promises, even of a royal commission. They ask government and parliament to deal, as they are in duty bound to deal, with Maritime interests, and to give those provinces a like measure of consideration as it meted out to the other provinces without the intervention of royal commissions.
The summary I have in mind, and which I do not say wholly covers the ground, might be briefly stated as follows:
(a)	That the integrity of the Intercolonial railway be restored with its western terminus at Montreal ;
(b)	That the service of that railway be what it was built for and intended to be when confederation was consummated-the connecting business link of the Maritimes with the central and other provinces;
(c)	That freight rates on the Intercolonial and other government lines east of Montreal be adjusted to carry out these purposes iu good faith; to enable products to flow from the Maritime provinces to those other provinces, and thus contribute to the development of industry in the Maritimes;
(d)	That good faith be kept by the observance of agreements, statutes and publicly given pledges in respect to the National Transcontinental railway which was to develop Canadian business, and force it, if necessary, through Canadian channels and Canadian ports;
(e)	That Maritime ports be satisfactorily equipped for export and import business, and particularly that ample cold storage accommodation be provided at the port of Halifax, as a part of the equipment of the National Railways;
(f)	That the agricultural, manufacturing and coal mining industries of the provinces, in common with the rest of Canada, be given tariff protection sufficient to safeguard enterprises of the people against unfair competition from mass production, cheap labour and depressed currency in other parts of the world, and preserve home markets for home producers;
(g)	That the Maritimes be put on a level with other provinces in the matter of the immigration and colonization enterprises of the government. In this matter the Maritimes have been ignored for many years;
(h)	That in the readjustment of terms with other provinces in relation to public lands, and other natural resources restored or added to those other provinces as the case may be, the rights of the Maritimes be recognized, and justice be done.
I have outlined somewhat fully the basis of the claims for the Maritimes, which I hope will be taken up and discussed more extensively by other hon. members.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to second the
resolution which has just been so admirably presented by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black). I wish, first of all, to state a principle. An essential principle to the life of the Dominion is that trade in Canada should be across the Dominion from east to west and from west to east, over Canadian rails and through Canadian ports. That is a principle which was affirmed at the time of confederation. It has been repeatedly stated in this House every year since confederation, but I feel that notwithstanding this repetition it is more necessary than ever that I should assert that principle in this House to-day. So much has been said, so much has been done and so little accomplished that I may well emphasize this principle of our Canadian Federation. The need of carrying it out is now more apparent and much greater than it ever was in years gone by. Therefore let me ask hon. members to keep in mind that vital principle lying at the basis of our dominion life as I have endeavored to express it.
Now, what has been done towards giving effect to this great principle? Much has been done. The Intercolonial has been built in accordance with the British North America Act, and later the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern were constructed. These
2312	COMMONS
Maritime Rights-Mr. MacLaren
two railways have cost the country hundreds of millions of dollars. Why were they built, and why did the country go to such enormous expense to assist in. their construction? The reasons are set out in the acts that my colleague from Halifax (Mr. Black) has already brought to the attention of the house. They were the acts of 1903 and 1914-one passed by a Liberal government, the other by a Conservative government. Surely, under these circumstances this government can rise to the occasion and accomplish what our predecessors undertook to do in the most solemn way. These acts would never have been passed by parliament had they not contained the principles which I am trying to advocate at the present moment, for they laid down the reasons for granting assistance and exacted from the two railways certain undertakings in return for that assistance. I need not set those undertakings out in detail, they have been brought to the attention of the House many times; briefly, these railways bound themselves to do all they could to further Canadian trade and as little as they could to assist competing trade.
I should like to supplement the statement in just two particulars. In reference to tonnage, in the act of 1903 there is embodied an agreement that the Grand Trunk Pacific will furnish, both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, all necessary tonnage to meet the demands of the country. Further, in the act of 1914 there is a very stringent provision with regard to the routing of freight by the Canadian Northern Railway. It is not a matter of choice with shippers or with the railroad but it is laid down that all freight for overseas, carried by the Canadian Northern, shall proceed over Canadian rails and through Canadian ports.
Of course, we all know that these railways have been taken over by the government and now form part of our Canadian National railway system. Consequently the board of directors has become responsible as successor for the obligations and agreements contained in the legislation of 1903 and 1914 on the part of those who then represented the Transcontinental and Canadian Northern railways Can we imagine anything otherwise? Is it to be suggested for a moment that the government or parliament would not proceed to honor the undertakings that they demanded and obtained from the railway managements of those days in return for the financial assistance then granted? We know that the legislation embodying those undertakings would never have passed parliament if it had been considered that they were worthless. Therefore I submit that as successors to the

companies that entered into those agreements, the board of directors of the Canadian National railways is legally responsible to honour them. Whether the House agrees with me on that point or not, surely it will be admitted that the good faith of parliament is at stake to see that the provisions embodied in those acts are duly observed.
Now, what has happened? Let me bring to the attention of -the House what Sir Henry Thornton, the chairman of the board of directors of the Canadian National railways, stated in public. Dealing with rates and the encouragement of Canadian trade, he said:	This high policy must be with the
government and with parliament. He and his directors regard the Canadian National railway system as separate and distinct from the rest of our national organizations, and as such they are operating it. But that system is not to be so treated, for it is an integral portion of the life of this country and indeed of its very existence. Surely neither the House nor the country would wish the Canadian National railway system to be managed without due regard to the interests of the nation as a whole. Our national railways form an essential portion of our national fabric and as such must be managed; that is, with due regard to the interests of the whole country, whether the system is apparently paying or not. Far greater questions than railway deficits or surpluses arise in this connection. I believe that greater financial success would result to the Dominion generally from operating our national railways from a truly national standpoint than in an endeavour to secure an operating surplus railroading-as is now being done-two thirds of our grain to foreign ports, and forty per cent of our total export traffic overseas over American rails and through American ports.
A few days ago, when this matter of rates was being considered by the railway commission, especially in relation to the Transcontinental, a reduction of freight rates was vigorously opposed-by whom do you think? By the Canadian National railway management. That does not look as if the board of directors of our national system was trying to carry out the principles embodied in the legislation to which I have referred. Those principles are not being observed in our transportation, and one can come to no other conclusion than that we cannot depend on the Canadian National railway board to give effect to those principles. I do not altogether blame the management for their action. I think they are trying to do their best to operate the system as they think it should be

Maritime Rights-Mr. MacLaren
operated, but while they entertain their present views of what is essential in railway operation, there seems to be no prospect whatever of the principles laid down in the acts of 1903 and 1914 being translated into practice.
Now wdiat remains? I submit that only one thing remains under these circumstances, and that is for the government of the country to step in and deal with this matter, which is essentially a governmental matter. It is a matter of high policy; it is a matter on which the welfare of this country depends, and one which is causing a great deal of unrest at the present time. I trust the government will not allow these troubles to seethe and grow', but will exercise that great responsibility which is placed in the hands of a government, and that is to formulate policies and carry them out. But the government have formulated no policy. I have heard and seen nothing they have enunciated as to this problem. What have they done? They say that they are placing these questions in the hands of a royal commission to make a finding, and in that way they hope to meet the situation. Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with that view. On no occasion, in the history of this parliament has the Maritime situation been so frequently presented to the House as during this session, and I am not aware of any member of this House having asked for such a commission. It is true that the government does not require to consult the members as such, but, on the other hand, when there is here a large number of men who are deeply interested in this question, men who have been sent here by the people to present their views, surely it would be in order to look for some other way of meeting this situation in the beginning.
I do not say, Mr. Speaker, that a royal commission can be of no use in such a matter. I can conceive that it could be useful if necessary in determining points at issue, once the principle and policy have been determined by the government, but I do not see how it is possible for a commission to deal with the various questions that certainly will be presented to them if they now proceed to function. I and many others have been sent to this parliament to press this subject as forcibly as we can. There is only one body that I can look to, and that is this parliament and this government, and I would urge the government, and I feel fully warranted in doing so, to announce its policy on this matter, so that if we are going to have the royal commission it will have a chance to perform a useful function. Surely it is the
function of a government to express its policy in broad terms, especially on such a question as this, which is a broad Canadian national question. That surely is the function of a government, and we look to the government to exercise that function. It will not do to pass the question along to a commission, however highly the government may regard it, when it is a question that should be determined bjr the representatives of the people in this House, namely, by the government of the country. We wish, especially those of us coming from the section of the country that is particularly concerned in this resolution, that an early announcement be made by the government-now, not in the future. Is a prompt decision not warranted by the history of this question, which has been before parliament after parliament, and has been pressed particularly before the present parliament? Is there anything new about it? Surely the government has had sufficient time to ponder deeply this matter and to be in a position to state what their views are.
Mr. Speaker, the trade that is passing from our country, going past our doors, so much to the loss of many parts of the country, some parts suffering more than others but all bearing the loss, is producing a very deep discontent in the country, and the people are not prepared to submit to any such policy as that from which we are now suffering. Surely it must be for the welfare of the country, and for the happiness and contentment of its people who are interested in the honourable carrying out of the country's commitments that we shall during this session hear from the Prime Minister as to what line he proposes to follow. May I, in conclusion, say to all the members of this House, who have heard this question stated and restated so many times, that I trust it will be possible to-day on this subject, which is no new subject at all, to be able to come to a vote endorsing the terms of the resolution as proposed bv the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black).
Mr. ROBERT K. SMITH (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to detain the House at any length in the few remarks I have to make on the resolution as proposed by the senior member for Halifax (Mi. Black). I do wish to say, however, at the outset, that the hon. member for Halifax is to be heartily congratulated on having brought this matter to the attention of this House on various occasions. It is regrettable that in the past the House has not seen fit to deal with this very important question as

Maritime Rights-Mr. Smith
it should have been dealt with, and I do feel that had any measure of consideration been given in the past to the subject matter of this very important resolution, we would not be struggling as hard as we are to-day in the Maritime provinces under the burdens which are pressing so heavily on our shoulders.
The resolution I think can be very briefly considered under a few headings, and the first heading that I would like to suggest for the consideration of the House is the nonpolitical aspect of this question. We lay no blame at the door of any political party in particular for the non-fulfilment of the pledges of confederation, of pre-confederation, and of parliamentary commitments after confederation, but we do lay blame on all political parties in Canada for the nonfulfilment of these pledges. Bearing in mind that both political parties in this country are committed to the subject embodied in this important resolution, I think we can very happily approach the question in the spirit of a non-political atmosphere. In that way I feel I am perfectly within bounds in appealing to every hon. member and to every party represented in this House to consider this resolution purely from the non-political aspect and not from the attitude of political partisanship.
The second heading to which I would like to allude is the national character of the features embodied in the resolution. It is quite true that the Maritime provinces are specifically mentioned, but a broader aspect is also embodied in the resolution, and that has reference to the east and west trade in this Dominion. We cannot hope to develop trade in Canada by adhering strictly, as we have done in the past, to a policy of trade routing north and south. That has been to the detriment of certain portions of this Dominion. If that policy continues in force the billions of dollars that have been expended by the people of Canada to develop our railway system, to develop terminal ports and, in a transportation sense, to feed every portion of the Dominion will have gone for naught, will have been virtually lost. Unless we go back to the policy for which these railroads were constructed, go back to the pre-confederation promises, go back to the promises of the Fathers of Confederation and the parliamentary commitments of the past, then these colossal expenditures will not accomplish the object for which they were intended. So that we can very properly appeal for support for this movement on the ground of the large national question which is involved, divorced from any sectional feature.

The movement is national in its scope. Unless we develop east and west trade in Canada then the benefits will not accrue to the country which have been anticipated, promised and expected.
The third aspect of this question to which I wish to devote my attention is the financial one. It may be stated, no doubt it will be, that if the terms of the resolution are carried out in their entirety it will involve a burden that will weigh somewhat heavily upon the taxpayers of this country. Admitting for the sake of argument that some financial sacrifice to the rest of the Dominion will be involved if this policy is carried out, will it not in the end prove a benefit to the whole of the Dominion on the development of a larger volume of trade, in directing the railways to the project and to the development of the business for which they were inaugurated? If we create the anticipated volume of trade, if we bring shipping and tonnage to our terminal ports, and all our railway lines are fed with traffic from the east and west instead of following the north and south policy, it seems to me that will more than compensate us for any little sacrifice entailed by whatever contribution Canada makes for this undertaking. If we have to consider national questions purely from the standpoint of dollars and cents it seems to me that we cannot possibly hope to build up a united and satisfied country. Let me illustrate what I mean by this. Suppose we send our Children to the schools of "the United States to be educated because those schools happened to be cheaper than our own schools. If we did that we would not be following the policy inaugurated by our forefathers neither would we be observing British or Canadian traditions. We might get our children educated more cheaply, but they would be taught the Yankeeism of the schools across the border, they would be robbed of the privilege of being educated in British institutions-in a word such a thing would be opposed to the best British and Canadian traditions. 'It might be cheaper to do such a thing, but we do not pursue such a course and we are not going to do so for any such reason. The same can be said with respect to products and goods produced in Canada. We might buy all our goods in the United States or in some other foreign country because it might be cheaper to do so; but I do not think the Canadian people will ever support a policy of that kind because it would not tend to build up this country of which we are so proud, it would not develop Canada as a nation within the British Empire, but would have the very reverse effect. So it seems to me that if we are e'.'er to huild ud Canada

Alarilime Rights-Mr. Smith
we must not approach such questions as this purely from the standpoint of dollars and cents; we must study and follow the national aspect of a question like this with a clear vision which will enable us to look into the future.
Another heading upon which I intended to speak, but which has been dealt with ably by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) was the question of the promises of preconfederation and confederation times with . respect to the building of the Intercolonial railway. The hon. member has already quoted to you the remarks made in 1864 by some of the Fathers of Confederation. He has read to you some of the parliamentary commitments embodied in the statutes. He has cited remarks made by leaders of both political parties in this country. It seems to me that it would be fruitless to pursue that argument further because it is acknowledged by all that the real intention of the building of the Intercolonial primarily has not been carried out. The real purpose of the Intercolonial was to connect the markets of the Maritime provinces with the markets of central Canada but this purpose has never been fulfilled. In this connection I may be permitted to quote from a speech made in 1922 by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), and I may say that I am in hearty accord with the expressions to which he gave utterance on that occasion. He brought the subject up for the purpose of showing the difficulties under which we in the eastern portion of the Dominion laboured with respect !to our freight rates, and he gave utterance to certain remarks which will be found at page 3570 of revised Hansard of 1922. The hon. minister said:
Let me give you some illustrations of the increases that were put into effect in the eastern part of Canada as pointed out by the representatives of these provincial governments before the committee. The rate on lumber was increased 90 per cent. The rate on pulpwood was increased 95 per cent, and on fruit 65 per cent. The rate on potatoes was increased from 75 to 100 per cent, varying according to the distances which they were carried. Coal rates were increased from 80 to 138 per cent.
Then the minister gave the case of Spring-hill mines, 188 miles from Bathurst:
Industries in Bathurst,-
He stated.
-'find it possible to buy coal in Norfolk, West Virginia, and have it carried through the north Atlantic and gulf of St. Lawrence to Bathurst and discharged at less cost for transportation than would be the case if they obtained it from Springhill.
The minister went on to say:
Then, the increase in the rates on wire nails was from 80 to 111 per cent. The rates on sugar, which the Maritime provinces are specially qualified to handle on
account of their proximity to the West Indies, were increased nearly 300 per cent.
Turning to cotton duck products he said:
In the constituency of the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Hatfield) the cotton duck industry has been carried on for many years; the increase in the freight rates on the products of that industry has been 280 per cent. The result is that it has been practically impossible to carry on their business in other parts of Canada.
It will be seen that we have been loaded down with an increase of freight rates, and it is no 'wonder that there is commercial stagnation in the Maritime provinces to-day. The situation must be met and dealt with by this parliament. There is no other authority in the land, that I know of, that can deal with this very important matter. I say this particularly on account of what transpired at a recent hearing by the railway commission at Moncton. An application was made for a reduction in the freight rates on products of the Maritime provinces, and what do wre find? In the first instance, the counsel of the Canadian National Railways came before the railway commission contending that the Intercolonial railway was not built for the purpose of conveying the products of the Maritime provinces to the markets of central and western Canada, but contending, in opposition to the views expressed by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), who has quoted the expressions of the Fathers of Confederation and others, that the road was built for the purpose of conveying the products of central Canada and other portions of the Dominion to the Maritime provinces. The argument of counsel for the Canadian National before the railway commission was that we were to provide markets in the Maritime provinces for the central and western portions of Canada by the construction of the Intercolonal which is absolutely absurd and opposed to all statements bearing upon confederation both before and after the event. Not only that, but at this same meeting of the commission in Moncton, one of the traffic agents of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways argued that no reduction could be made in freight rates in the Atlantic region of the Canadian National because there was a deficit in that region. Now, Mr. Speaker, we expected a deficit on that portion of the road. After they cut off the old Intercolonial at Riviere du Loup, instead of extending it to Montreal, we expected there would be a deficit, for the very sane and logical reason that they cut off the paying and largest producing portion, and gave us the section that was not so productive. So that it is not at all surprising to us in the Maritime provinces that we have a deficit on the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Cahan
These were the reasons given by them why we should not be granted lower freight rates.
I desire to repeat what I said at the outset that I think this matter should be approached in a national way and from a non-political standpoint, and I think if it is considered in that manner it will be treated as an all-Canadian subject worthy of the consideration of all hon. members in this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
My only excuse, Mr. Speaker, for
trespassing on the time of the House for the purpose of discussing this question is that I was born and bred in the Maritime provinces, and I have always maintained a personal and intimate association with the province in which I was born. I do not intend to review the pre-confederation compact, because that is well known. I do not intend to praise or blame either of the successive administrations, because in my personal opinion they have each and all failed in originating and carrying into action an effective policy for the preservation of the industrial and commercial interests of the Maritime provinces and consolidating the political union which was framed in 1867.
I passed through one secession campaign in Nova Scotia, and I hope we will never see another. It is utterly unnecessary that there should be such a conflict of opinion and interest between any one of the Maritime provinces and the other provinces of the Dominion as to form any reasonable basis for a repeal campaign such as the one we went through in 1886 and 1887. But it does seem to me that the reference of a number of these matters to the commission recently appointed cannot result in any effective and satisfactory solution of these problems, unless the principles upon which that commission is to proceed are clearly determined and announced by the government of the day. I know that the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) must have as earnest a desire as any hon. member in this House to secure a fair and reasonable solution of these problems. Time and time again he has gone to the Maritime provinces and announced openly, and I believe sincerely, that he had a deep interest in the solution of the problems which confront these provinces. I give him credit for that, and I believe he has the same sincere and earnest desire to-day. Admitting that I would suggest to him, how can this commission recently appointed proceed without having a pre-determination of the problems which are presented to them? Are we going to have a kindergarten entertainment and 
take six or eight months in order to present the problems to the gentleman who will probably be chairman of that commission, and who is, I think, a very estimable man? But it will be a kindergarten entertainment before he can become thoroughly acquainted with the conditions, economic, transportation, commercial, industrial and otherwise, which confront these provinces, and especially Nova Scotia. Before that commission can proceed earnestly and efficiently to do its work, we must have a declaration on the part of the government in regard to the problems to be dealt with, and when I say the government I mean parliament as well, because any declaration of the government must be upheld by parliament to prove effective. Therefore we must have a clear declaration by the government and parliament upon the great industrial problem of conserving the iron and coal interests of those provinces. That is a tariff question, and it seems to me utterly useless to relegate that question to a commission, until the policy of the government and parliament is clearly enunciated in respect thereto.
Every hon. member who has lived through the history of confederation and taken partin it, as many in this House have, knows that it has been the policy of both parties to develop our commerce east and west, and on each and every occasion that the question of developing eastern and western traffic has arisen we have had pronouncements by the leaders of the Liberal party as well as by the Conservative leaders that they regarded it as the bounden duty and obligation of parliament to encourage by every means, the transfer of Canadian freight and Canadian products through Canadian ports. No clearer enunciation of that policy could possibly be given than that contained in the Grand Trunk Pacific agreement dealing with the traffic over the Transcontinental railway, laid before this House in the session of 1903. I would desire to refer to section 42 and other relevant sections which were incorporated in that agreement. They were so highly approved by the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding who then held an eminent position in the government of that day, so heartily endorsed by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the leader of the government of that day, that a tremendous impression was made upon the people of the Maritime provinces and they felt that whatever lapses might have occurred in the past, from that time forward the government and parliament of Canada would, in the exercise of their wisdom, inaugurate such measures, industrial, commercial, traffic,

trade, transportation, as to ensure that the traffic of the west would be carried through Maritime province ports. Section 42 of that agreement, which is found as an addenda or an appendix to chapter 71 of the acts of parliament of 1903, states:
42. It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian 'trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid under these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall!, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time bo greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not sipeeificaAly routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
There are a number of other sections of that agreement which carry out exactly the same intention. Before this question of freight rates can even be examined effectively by the Board of Railway Commissioners, we must have a clear declaration binding on them by the government and parliament of this country as to the policy of parliament with respect to the freight rate which may be inaugurated. First, is there to be one freight rate structure for the whole of Canada and binding the whole of the Canadian National Railways, or is there to be, as there was prior to a few years ago, a distinctive and independent freight rate structure over the lines from Montreal east, which prior to that date were fixed and from time to time changed and modified for the express purpose of building up provincial trade between the ports of St John, Halifax, Sydney and Montreal? That issue is one that cannot be settled under present conditions by the Board of Railway Commissioners, nor is it a question that can be effectively investigated and reported upon by the new commission recently appointed, until it is predetermined what is the policy of this government and parliament with respect thereto. That is one point upon which there must be a clear understanding.
We have the further question which is very interesting to the Maritime provinces, and that is as to the conditions under which the Transcontinental line will be operated from Prince Rupert to the port of Quebec and from the port of Quebec to Moncton, its terminus in the Martime provinces. That line, built at such a great expense, upon which the hopes of ail the people of Canada rested at the time, a project that was received with enthusiasm from one end of Canada to the other, an enthusiasm due largely to the earn-
Maritime Rights-Mr. Cahan
est and, I believe, sincere advocacy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier-that line, built across the continent on the lowest grade of any transcontinental line in North America, is lying practically idle because the government and parliament of the day have never determined the conditions under which it shall be operated, what will be the rate structure for freights over it, or whether it will be used to carry grain to the port of Quebec and to build up a second ocean port there.	The
traffic of this country in a few years will be quite sufficient for Quebec as well as for Montreal. Shall it be operated across the bridge and down through New Brunswick for the purpose of building up Canadian ports during the winter? Is it possible for the government to announce its policy with respect to that? That policy must be clearly determined before we can hope to secure any satisfactory results either from the Board of Railway Co'mmisisioiners or from the new commission which has been recently appointed to inquire into conditions which prevail in the Maritime provinces.
There are other questions. I do not wish to go beyond the purport of this resolution, but if I might be allowed I should like to make a criticism and an altogether friendly one because this question is one that commands the most earnest attention, the most patriotic endeavour of both sides of this House. It is not a question which should be put forward for any mere partisan purpose. It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. I think my hon. friend would find that the House would agree that the rates from west to east must be considered. Quotations have been made from the speeches of Sir George Etienne Cartier and Hon. George Brown in which these gentlemen spoke of Upper Canada sending its farm and manufactured products to the Maritime provinces while the latter in return shipped its coal and fish westward. I assume that was the intention so far as those gentlemen were concerned. On referring to the statute, section 145 of the British North America Act, which provided for the construction of the Intercolonial railway, I find the following:
Intercolonial Railway
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have joined in a declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial railway is essential to the consolidation of the union of British North America, and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and have consequently agreed that provision should be made for its immediate construction by the government of Canada: Therefore, in order to give effect to that agreement, it shall be the duty of the government and parliament of Canada to provide for the commencement, within six months after the union, of a railway connecting the river St. Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, and for the construction thereof without intermission, and the completion thereof with all practicable speed.
Now let us see what the history of that project was. The railway was constructed by the government of Canada under that statute, utilizing the existing portions of railway in the Maritime provinces, to Riviere du Loup, the original terminus of the Intercolonial. I well remember attending a meeting at Halifax which was addressed by Sir Charles Tupper and the Hon. A. G. Jones, when the subject of discussion was the probability of Halifax becoming the winter port of the Dominion, although the Intercolonial at that time went only to Riviere du Loup. Later on the government extended the line to Levis, and in 1898, when the late Mr. Blair was Minister of Railways, owing to the acquisition of the Drummond county railway, a further extension took place to Montreal.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Macdonald (Anlig.)
There is nothing in the statute from which I have quoted which makes any reference one way or the other to railway rates; but from the time of the completion of the railway down to 1912, when the first increase of railway rates took place, the Intercolonial was operated in accordance with what hon. gentlemen opposite assert to have been the intent of the Fathers of Confederation: we had rates that enabled our products to find access to central Canada, and an interprovincial trade existed which was highly satisfactory. In addition to through rates that were not high, very satisfactory local rates were granted which permitted of an exchange of products between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. At that time New Brunswick had no coal and we had an abundant supply; and there were other conditions which permitted of an interchange of products and enabled our people to prosper to a fairly satisfactory degree. I think it was in 1912, when the late Mr. Cochrane was Minister of Railways, that the first increase in rates came; it was largely an increase in local rates. In 1918 or 1919 a new classification of rates was imposed on all parts of the Intercolonial, and there is no manner of doubt that since that time the rates imposed have had an injurious effect on our industries down there and have rendered it practically impossible for us to ship to central Canada those natural products which we can supply. But at no time have we ever had any record of these rights as being definitely and certainly determined. When hon. gentlemen speak about pre-confederation understandings in regard to rates they are not talking about railway rates, because those had not been determined; they are talking about interchange of trade and the maintenance of such rates as should be necessary to develop interprovincial trade. But for over forty years every consecutive government, whether Liberal or Conservative, recognized the rights of the people of the Maritime provinces to have the Intercolonial railway operated under the conditions which existed at the time referred to.
Now it is most essential that the people of Canada should know definitely, through some responsible authority, what those confederation understandings were and how they were interpreted by successive governments. There is only one way in which that could be done. My hon. friends opposite say they do not think the Maritime rights commission will result in any good. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) thought the commission would take a long time to acquaint itself with the economic 14011-14Si

Such representations relate more particularly to the alleged failure to use Canadian ports for Canadian trade to the extent to which they might be utilized-
There is a subject upon which this commission can report-whether or not the good faith of the country, pledged by these statutes in 1903, is being violated, and if so in what respect. This House can then adopt such means as are within its power to provide a remedy. The order proceeds:
-and to the handicaps said to result from the operation of the schedules of rates chargeable for the carriage of goods on the railways uniting the Maritime provinces with the other provinces of Canada and to the manner of administering that part of the Canadian National Railways system which was formerly known as the Intercolonial Railway by methods and conditions alleged to be inconsistent with the pledges given at the time of confederation in regard thereto, and with the practice followed from the time of the construction of the railway until December, 1918.
In other words, with regard to both branches of this resolution a commission has been constituted for the purpose of reporting to parliament whether, in the one case, the good faith of Canada has not been kept, and in the other, pre-confederation pledges have been disregarded in the conduct of the administration of the railway subsequent to confederation. I submit that the method we have adopted is the right and proper one, from the standpoint of those of us who live in the Maritime provinces and who want to secure the application of substantial and intelligent remedial measures in regard to our grievances. We do not want any jumping in the dark. We want our position in confederation clearly and definitely understood by parliament, so that lion, members coming from all parts of Canada may be able, when that report comes before them, to deal intelligently with the matter, and to assist in providing a suitable remedy.
I am glad to observe that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St, George refers to the personnel of the commission in complimentary terms. Nothing can be said derogatory to any of the gentlemen composing the com-

No journal in this country has been more vigorous and aggressive in demanding a recognition of what have been called Maritime rights than the Halifax Herald, and when the announcement of the appointment of the commission was made the other day, that paper published in large headlines :
Victory for Maritime rights. Federal Probe is Ordered.
Then on the following day they published an editorial which dealt in this way with the objections which had been mooted by hon. gentlemen here:
Now there is to be a federal royal commission to investigate all phases of Maritime rights. This is indeed a great victory for the earnest, devoted men and women of the Maritimes who persisted in their fight against indifference and discrimination abroad and discouraging propaganda at home. The leaders of the movement are now able to read in the order in council appointing a commission a recitation of the claims they have been pressing for years; and they know that this action by the federal government comes as the certain result of the work that has been carried on with such splendid courage and determination by those who were not daunted by indifference and discrimination on the one hand, nor discouraged by partisan propaganda on the other.
These representations contained in the Nova Scotia resolution are made to apply, in the federal order in council, to the three Maritime provinces, an application with which the people of this province will agree.
We realize that there are many in the Maritimes who doubt the efficacy at this late date of a royal commission, such as has been appointed at Ottawa.
Be that as it may, it is the opinion of the Halifax Herald that the Duncan commission, now it is formed and instructed to proceed with its investigation, should receive every co-operation and support from the Maritime people.
And I bespeak from hon. gentlemen who are m3" colleagues from the Maritime provinces in this House that co-operation and support in order that the commission may be a proper fact-finding commission, and that the report may be such as will command the confidence of the House and the country. The editorial continues:
The salvation of the Maritimes lies in co-operation-one million people speaking with one voice-and we trust that the people of the Maritimes will do everything in their power to further the work of the commission and bring to its deliberations such a volume and character of evidence and information as will establish beyond doubt the justice of Maritime claims. We feel it to be the duty of the governments of the three Maritime provinces to provide for representation before the commission; and a similar duty devolves upon other public bodies in the Maritimes, as well as upon all private citizens who may be able to contribute to the success of the inquiry.
It is not a question of individual views, nor of party politics; it is a question of Maritime betterment. And no matter what may be the opinions of our people upon the many economic and political questions involved, it is a duty of Maritime citizenship to co-

operate in this, as in all other features of the Maritime movement. After listening to some of the arguments that have been presented this afternoon, and particularly to the agreement which was read by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), there appeared to me to be strong argument and good reason why a thorough investigation should take place before there is any tinkering with railway rates, in order to ensure that grain shall pass through Canadian channels. I refer to the clause which says that Canadian grain shall not be carried to American ports at a rate less than that at which it is carried to Canadian ports. If I caught it aright, that is the statement. We will suppose that that applies to Montreal. How will it affect the shipper? I do not know whether this came into effect after the railways were carrying grain to Portland, Maine, and) to Sty John and Halifax lat different rates, but the effect in any case would be the same, Let us suppose a Shipper has a cargo of grain at Fort William.
Ordinarily, he would send it to Montreal, we will say, in the latter part of the season- this would not apply in the summer-and then he would get it to Portland for a cheap rate, because the distance is not great. This order is put into effect that (grain must not be carried to a United States port at a rate less than that at which it is carried to a Canadian port. If any of those gentlemen who are discussing this were railway officials, had the management of the railways affected, what would they do? I would just like to ask them. Would they not raise the rate to Portland and lower it to St. John and Halifax? The reasonable supposition is that they would cut the difference in two. That is, grain that would ordinarily be carried from Montreal to Portland for, say three cents-in order to illustrate my point-would probably cost five or six cents after this order goes into effect. I understood that it was at one time an order; I understand now it. is a part of the contract. The man who has the cargo of gram says: I cannot get it out to Portland, St. John or Halifax as cheaply as I used to or as I could if this clause was not in the agreement; what shall I do with it? I will send it out by Buffalo. That is, by putting that clause in your contract, by trying to keep grain in Canadian ,channels, you effect just the opposite; the clause defeats its purpose and drives the grain into the United States channels at Buffalo. It may be that I did not hear the statement exactly aright, but I believe I did and I have reason to fear that that will be the effect.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman not admit that the discriminatory rates over the Transcontinental have had the effect of diverting grain to United States ports?

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
That is an entirely different matter. I was coming to that later on. This will have and has the effect of driving grain into the United States at Buffalo rather than of keeping it in Canada as far as Montreal. I am speaking of the latter part of the season when the St. Lawrence is frozen and ships cannot leave that port. If you try to drive the grain to Halifax or St. John, several hundred1 miles further, by saying to the railways, not that it must be carried at the Portland rate or the Halifax or St. John rate, but that it must be Carried at the same rate, you will drive the grain out of Canada at Buffalo. I believe if hon. gentlemen look into the matter they will find that is the effect of it.
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) presented a strong case tinged less

Maritime Rights-Mr. Millar
with party politics than we are usually unfortunate enough to have to listen to in connection with this matter. He made the remark that it might be well for parts of Canada to make sacrifices in order that traffic might be sent to Halifax and St. John in order to build up the eastern provinces. I quite agree with him in that, provided that the sacrifice is not too great. If our railways are carrying Canadian traffic even at cost we should not forget that while the railway itself is not making money it is employing many men who are drawing full pay and if, as is suggested, some sacrifice is made even by those who grow the grain, if they pay a little more to have the grain kept in Canadian channels, the benefits they would get in an indirect way would! offset the heavier overhead in freight. But when you ask the grain grower to pay perhaps four or five cents or three cents more per bushel, you are asking something that he will not grant. He cannot concede that much.
Why does Canadian grain go through United States channels? Hecently I had pointed out to me some evidence taken by the Great Lakes commission and I noted questions asked of a representative of the shipping board. His answers showed that the rate on grain from Duluth to Buffalo was at that time about 34 cents a bushel while the rate over a much shorter route, from Fort William to Buffalo or Port Colborne, was 5 cents. There you have a difference of 14 cents a bushel. How are you going to say to the shipper: You must pay the higher rate? The government will have to take a high hand, become quite arbitrary, to force the shipper to send his grain by a certain route. He is going to take the cheaper route; the question is an economic one.
It has been contended in this House, I believe, that rates from New York to Liverpool and from Montreal to Liverpool are the same. I must take issue with that statement; the rate is usually less from New York than from Montreal. The rate on Canadian grain from Fort William to Liverpool b}? the United States route is practically always less than by the Canadian route. It is not an easy matter to overcome that. I would like to see Canadian grain go through Canadian channels, but I cannot think that is all the question in connection with the Maritime provinces. I listened to the case presented by three hundred representatives from there a year ago and I would get the impression from what they stated that there was nothing there except St. John and Halifax. I expect to hear something about the country, about the industries, about agriculture, but I heard

nothing about that; all I heard was about freight through Halifax and St. John. I cannot think the fact of grain travelling down past their doors, going through their province, being shipped from their harbours of Halifax and St. John, even if it all went there, is going to remedy their troubles, is going to put them on a sound economic basis. There must be other difficulties. I do not wish to say this as a matter of criticism, but I have listened too frequently to statements made as though contractual obligations were entered into at the time confederation was being negotiated, when to me they were simply pious hopes of what would or might take place if the Intercolonial railway were built. I think about ninety per cent of what have been spoken of as contractual obligations were simply pious hopes. I know two men who traded horses, and one of them slapped the other on the shoulder-he knew him very well-and said: "Jack,, if you get that horse he will surprise you." They were both horse traders. Jack got the horse and he certainly did surprise him because when he got out into the field he would kick himself clear of the harness. I think the Maritime righters are in the same predicament; they heard a great deal at that time of what should, and what they believed and hoped would, take place, and apparently they swallowed it all. But that is quite different from a contractual obligation.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) asked a question about the National Transcontinental Railway. I would have liked the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George i(!Mr. Cahan) to tell us that he was so anxious for a solution of this question that he would even favour cutting the rate on the Canaidan National from Armstrong, which is north of Fort William, so that it would be on a parity with the rate on grain in western Canada. That would bring it to about 11 cents or a trifle more; it is now 20.7 cents. However, the hon. member rather sidestepped that question I thought. If that rate were reduced it would be a great help, and I do not see any reason why that should not be done. That was the intention when the Transcontinental was built, with very good grades, heavy rails and well-built bridges fitted to carry heavy loads, yet with the exception of a very short period-I think some six months -the rate always has been prohibitive, so that no grain goes there and the grass i3 growing around the rails. If the rate were reduced to eleven cents I think the port of Quebec ,would be used very much more, and the two million bushel capacity there would be made some use of.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Cantley
This is a very difficult question, and it is well that it should be discussed in this House I for one am willing to listen to any arguments presented. The Maritime provinces art a part of Canada and we want to see their, prosper. Any assistance we can give in the solving of the problem will, I believe, receive the support of all members of the House; it will receive my support, at any rate. But we must approach the matter in a businesslike way, and we must face the facts. The amount of traffic over which the railway has control is small, I believe, in comparison to that over which the shipping interests have control, and so long as grain can be carried for a few cents less by the United States railways I am afraid they will get the business.
I would like to see the traffic kept in Canada, however, if that can be done.
