subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I had been referring to the necessity for an intercolonial railway if the several eastern provinces were to be brought into the confederation. All of us who are informed as to what was done at that time are thoroughly aware of what was promised in connection with the building and the subsequent operation and management of that Intercolonial railway. I shall not refer to that matter further.
I shall now deal with what the Maritime provinces have contributed towards the Canadian Pacific Railway and what benefit we in the east have derived from that great enterprise. The eastern provinces paid their share of the cost of the road, and, unfortunately for us in Nova Scotia, it ended at St. John. So far as Nova Soctia is concerned, this great transcontinental railway, so far as transportation and the advantages accruing from competition are concerned, might as well have been non-existent. Over a considerable period of years we in Nova Scotia, particularly the iron and steel plants of that country, and more particularly the Scotia Steel Company of New Glasgow were able to sell to the Canadian Pacific Railway very large quantities of railway material. As a matter of fact the Canadian Pacific Railway was by far our largest and most important customer. In the early days that railway took delivery of all material sold by the Scotia company to them at St. John, on equal terms with material delivered to them by other parties at Montreal or at Hamilton, as the case might be.
	i
But some time ago, due to a change of policy, the St. John Canadian Pacific Railway gateway was closed, and we were then unable to make delivery to the Canadian Pacific Railway at that point, the Canadian Government Railway insisting on getting the long haul. We therefore had to pay the freight, not to St. John, a distance of 255 miles, but to Montreal, some 800 miles. The Canadian Pacific Railway then naturally said to us: Inasmuch as you cannot now give us any traffic, we see no good reason why vre should now give business to you, more particularly in view of the fact that the other manufacturers in Ontario and Quebec who can give us freight, and who do give us freight, are clamouring for the business which you are asking us to give you. The result of this was that we were practically pushed out of the Canadian Pacific Railway business, due to unfair discrimination on the part of a railwty which was built to give us facilities for doing business in the central and western provinces.
Now the only effective cure for that condition that I know of would be to give, as at one time was contemplated, running rights to the Canadian Pacific Railway from St. John to Halifax and through New Glasgow eastward to the Sydneys. This is necessary if we in Nova Scotia are to get our fair share of the business given out by that railway-and it must be remembered that the two railways of Canada are by far the largest and most important consumers of iron and steel products in this country-and it is essential that we be put in a position to make deliveries on the lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway as I have indicated.
Now I refer to another matter. Owing to territorial concessions t>o other provinces and certain changes in the distribution of population, largely due to the exodus of the population of the Maritime provinces to the west, it is imperative that the Maritime representation in the Dominion parliament be now readjusted so that our voice and prestige in the Dominion parliament be adequately maintained. What is necessary to-day is to restore representation in the federal parliament in the proportion set forth in section 37 of the British North America Act. The Maritime provinces contend that they have a proprietary interest in the natural resources of the former Northwest Territories. They maintain that they should and must be recompensed for that portion of the territory in question which has been ceded to other provinces, and from which it is now proposed to make further transfers, although no compensation has been or is proposed to be given to the Maritime provinces for such transfers.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Cantley
There has grown up a deep feeling of discontent in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick during the past few years with regard to the relations existing between these provinces and the Dominion as a whole. This feeling has been increased by the apparent indifference with which appeals for fair treatment have been received, coupled with the other grievances to which I have referred- the reduced representation in parliament accorded those provinces, particularly Nova Scotia. What we are now asking is a fair and honest recognition of our rights and interests in view of the fact that but for Nova Scotia, the oldest province in the Dominion, confederation and the creation of the Dominion of Canada would have been impossible.
I do not think it is necessary to enlarge on the fact that but for the entry of Nova Scotia into confederation the federation compact would have been impossible. For five months in the year this Dominion is dependent entirely on these two provinces for access to the sea. That was demonstrated, as I have already pointed out, during the war. Surely we have not forgotten the lesson then impressed upon us. Surely we are prepared to pay those Maritime provinces a fair consideration for the position that they occupy and the difficulties which they have encountered as members of confederation. Prior to confederation we Nova Scotians were a prosperous people. Nova Scotia then stood fourth amongst the shipowning nations of the world, possessing more shipping property per capita than any nation on the globe. Our flag-and Nova Scotia alone of all the dominions then had a flag-our white ensign with the blue cross of St. Andrew, was shown on every sea. We had freighters on the Atlantic. Far up the Rio Grande, and all the ports and rivers of South America were equally familiar to our captains, our seamen, and! our ships, Nova Scotia shipping was to be found on all the trade routes of the world. Now, I do not say that confederation is responsible for the ruining of that trade and the disappearance of our shipping. The transition from wooden to iron bottoms, and later on the victory of the steel tramp steamer over the steel sailing vessel wiped out our wooden fleet. Then came confederation with its inducements as to our being able to transport our products and manufactures over the Intercolonial to the central and western provinces. Those suggestions turned our thoughts to other employment, and instead of taking up the building of a fleet of steel steamers as we should have done and could have done readily-and
as was done by Norway first and later by Holland-and thus maintaining our supremacy in the transport of traffic and navigation throughout the world for which we were admirably adapted by nature, we sold our fleets largely to the Norwegians and spent the proceeds, supplemented by our savings in the building of sugar refineries, cotton mills, iron and steel furnaces and mills, the products of which we were assured were to be carried by the Intercolonial to Upper Canada, a thing to be rendered possible by special freight rates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, isolated on the extreme east of Canada, and separated from Quebec by 500 miles practically of wilderness in which no trade for the Maritime provinces exists, we were promised a differential which is now nonexistent. To-day we are charged full mileage rates which are from 100 to 150 per cent greater than those in effect twelve years ago, and in not a few cases the westbound rates are higher than the eastbound rates. This is in absolute contradiction indeed a complete reversal of the promises made to us. All protests so far made as to this unfair treatment have been ignored or denied. Our whole freight traffic structure is controlled and administered to-day by a few old Grand Trunk officials established in Montreal who view the Maritimes from the background of Chicago, Portland and New London instead of in the light of the industrial interests of Amherst, New Glasgow the Sydneys and the other manufacturing towns of the east. Due to competition with the mass production of the industries of Quebec and Ontario, and unequal and oppressive freight rates, it is now impossible to carry on many of the enterprises to which I have referred. Enterprises which were entered into a few years ago with a good deal of enthusiasm have now come to grief, with loss of much of the capital invested therein. Another difficulty with which we have to contend is that the steel duties have been so dealt with as to make them practically of little or no value to the industries of the Maritime provinces. MoTe than three score of items have been taken from the dutiable schedule and put in the free list, and to-day there is practically nothing on which we have protection worth mentioning outside of the one item of railway materials. We have been sacrificed to the manufacturers elsewhere, to the implement people of Canada, to the interests of anybody who had some pull or made pretensions to do something at the expense of somebody else.
Prior to confederation our coal went largely to the New England states. Fifty years ago
Maritime Rights-Mr. Cantley

over a thousand vessels loaded every summer in the port of Pietou for the New England ports and almost as many in the port of Sydney for the same market. Had it not been for confederation we would have been able to establish satisfactory and permanent arrangements and connections with American capital, with American railways, with American manufacturers, principally in the New England states, and would have done so. Thus we would have secured an all-the-year-round market for our coal. After the monopoly of the General Mining Association of London was broken up in 1856 it was American capital that developed our collieries, not Canadian, or European, or British capital. The only exception to that statement was in the case of one colliery in Cumberland county, one in Pietou county and possibly one in Cape Breton.
It is said that we in Nova Scotia are trading unnaturally and there may be some truth in that statement. But whether or not it be the case, the fact is that we are trading to-day as we are forced to do, and have been for fifty years been forced to do through our being included in the Dominion of Canada. This virtually means that Nova Scotia has been sacrificed to the consolidation of the empire. Unfortunately the Dominion as a whole treats Nova Scotia in the main as the empire has always treated its soldiers, relying on them in time of war and forgetting and neglecting them in time of peace. That has been our fortune-just the same treatment a3 the empire from time immemorial has accorded the men who fought for and defended the empire in time of stress. We were told within the last day or two by an eminent advocate speaking in this city, who dealing with the present political situation, said that the cleft as between the east and the rest of Canada is not permanent and can be cured when the Maritimes take again to the toil of their forefathers. I wonder if he knew the meaning of his own statement? In effect, he suggests that after contributing to confederation, having contributed-millions of dollars to the various railway enterprises in the central and western provinces and in manufacturing industries in our own provinces, dependent entirely upon equal trading advantages as compared with the. central provinces, first as to transportation and second to tariff protection, we are now to scrap all our manufactures, lose the millions which we have invested, the savings of a century of toil, go back to wooden ships, make a futile effort to regain our lost position as world carriers and be content to be further exploited by the manufacturers, 
the millers and the food producers west of the St. Lawrence river.
This matter of justice to the Maritimes is not a local dispute, such as that between a industrial. corporation and its workers or between a railway system and its operatives. It is rather a case of long standing dissatisfaction, due to years of disregard of understandings, pledges and promises incidental to and arising out of confederation-unequal contribution and commitments as to railway construction, and the relatively small proportion of benefits and advantages accruing to the eastern provinces; our contributions to and our obligations resulting from the Maritime proportionate contribution to and share of the construction and share of the operative loss on the great canal system of Canada. This system, which cost $225,000,000, has been operated entirely for the benefit of the central and western provinces, with only this exception, that to some considerable extent the United States coal and steel producers, who are our great competitors, are accorded free transport on these same canals, the operating loss of which is equally borne by us -with the other provinces; fancy Americans given free transport facilities, at our expense, to compete with ourselves in the central provinces of Canada. If any more ludicrous trade conditions can exist it is impossible for me to conceive of them. We are subject to all these conditions, and no attention whatever, over a long period of years, has been given to any objection we have made in regard to them. We have called the attention of government after government and parliament after parliament, one set of ministers after another, to the unequal and unfair treatment which we have been accorded in that connection. The unequal advantage accruing to the central provinces from the present unfair operation of the tariff and the greatly preponderating advantages which the central sections of the Dominion derive from it is another matter of which we complain. In that regard we expect and have a right to expect that justice shall be accorded us. Then there is the failure to recognize the undoubted rights of the Maritime provinces in the lands already alienated and now proposed to be further alienated from the federal domain. These and some other federal questions, and the situation arising out of them, are so far reaching and so vitally important to the wellbeing of the provinces and confederacy a3 to put the whole matter quite beyond the range of questions that can or should be dealt with by a commission.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Brown
I have no present intention to here or now attack the personnel of the proposed commission, but for the weighty reasons I have referred to and others equally important we decline to submit our case to or to be in any way guided or obligated by any findings arising out of an investigation by such a commission. On the contrary we ask for, indeed we demand, a parliamentary committee to which we can appeal, as in the case of the Crowsnest pass rate question, which was considered and dealt with by such a committee in the year 1922; and that is not so far back but that most of the members of this House are quite familiar with the question and the settlement arrived at as to the matters then in dispute. Failure to meet the demands of Nova Scotia will tend to make of that province another Ireland, with an accompaniment of ill feeling, trouble and loss as between the eastern provinces and the Dominion greater and more far reaching than any disturbance which has arisen in the past out of the Irish question. Some hon. members opposite may laugh, but I can assure them it is no laughing matter. It is a matter which should receive the serious consideration of this House and unless it does receive such consideration there is trouble in store for this country; as to that there is no possibility of doubt.
I again tell the government we do not want a commission. We ask and demand that the matter of our grievances be examined by a committee of this House. The responsibility is on the government and to them the provinces by the sea look for relief, failing which this government must and will be held responsible for consequences that will affect not Nova Scotia alone but the whole of this Dominion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would scarcely have taken part in this debate were it not for the fact that I represent a constituency in the province which, of all the provinces, has perhaps suffered the most through the failure of Canada to carry out the terms of confederation and, as the resolution puts it, "to keep faith with the assurances and undertakings of the government and parliament of Canada." I do not intend to cover the ground of the resolution generally, but to refer briefly to some parts that apply particularly to the province of Prince Edward Island.

Prince Edward Island held out for better terms than those originally proposed in 1867, and having secured them entered Confederation in 1873. At that time the island had been a self-governing colony for over one hundred years, and in the interval had made great progress. People from the Old Country settled there and hewed farms out of the wilderness and eventually became prosperous. They developed a thriving trade and established industries suitable to their needs, such as cloth mills, knitting mills, boot and shoe factories and agricultural implement factories. In the thirty years before confederation the population doubled itself, the revenues were ouoyant and sufficient in every way to meet the colony's expenditure.
Now, the last speaker (Mr. Brown) asked in what way the terms of confederation were not carried out. One of the terms under which Prince Edward Island entered the Dominion was:
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the Island and the mainland, winter and Summer, thus placing the Island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the hon. member: Does he know how faith was kept with Prince Edward Island with respect to that term of the union? We suffered for many years under the failure of Canada to carry out that part of the bargain. In 1900, under the Laurier government, the claims of Prince Edward Island for damages in that regard were recognized, and the government of that day granted an additional subsidy of $30,000 a year in settlement of all claims on that account up to 1900. That represented probably a capital sum of a million dollars at that time. But would any hon. member say that a million dollars would compensate for the hardships we suffered for twenty-seven long years by reason of that failure of Canada to carry out that term of the confederation pact?
But suppose we say we were adequately settled with up to 1900, I would point out to the House some of the things that happened later. In the winter of 1902-03 we were 35 days without steam connection of any kind with the mainland, and 33 days during which there was only a one-way or a half-trip service: in the winter of 1904-05 we were 54 days without any steamer communication with the mainland and were 19 days with only a one-way or half-trip service, while for 21 days we never received any mail from the mainland; in the winter of 1906-07 we were

Maritime Rights-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
thirty-five days without any communication with the mainland. Yet we entered confederation on the distinct understanding with the Dominion government that we would be furnished with an efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers continuously throughout the year between the Island and the mainland. I ask the hon. member: In the face of these facts does he think Prince Edward Island was fairly treated? Why, sir, under the conditions I have described between 1900 and the present time our trade has fallen off through the non-fulfilment of this particular term of the contract, and as a result many firms have gone into bankruptcy owing to losses incurred by destruction of perishable products through delay in transportation. These disastrous conditions have seriously injured our people, until to-day our former thriving industries are a mere memory and our population has dwindled from practically a hundred thousand people in 1873 to less than 90,000 to-day.
Now, this is one of the failures of Canada to implement its promises that we think should be dealt with. Whether the royal commission that has been appointed will deal with our grievances fully and fairly is something that I do not care to discuss. I do feel, however, that we should not be put off with a royal commission, that the facts can be fairly represented to the government by the members of this House and by the provincial governments of the three maritime provinces. The three premiers are now engaged in preparing the case of the maritimes for presentation to the federal government. I know that the premier of Prince Edward Island, in conjunction with the premiers of Nova and New Brunswick, has been working on the case for two years. I believe that those gentlemen and the members in this House representing the maritime provinces are in a far better position than any royal commission to present to the federal government our local needs and claims.
While our claims have much in common with those of the other two maritime provinces, we have a claim peculiar to the Island; I refer to our mainland connection, which is not yet satisfactory. Although in 1912 the Borden government made a start to implement this clause of the confederation agreement, even to-day our communication with the mainland is not entirely satisfactory, but I am ready to admit that it is much better than it used to be. I am not citing the action of the Borden government for political reasons, because I am quite ready to give the Laurier government credit for recognizing our
Claims in 1900, but the Borden government went a long way to improve con-9 p.m. ditions when they began to standardize our railway and provide a car ferry service. But what is the condition to-day? More than half of the Prince Edward Island railway is still narrow gauge, and hon. members, unless they have had the experience of handling traffic from a narrow gauge to a standard gauge line, cannot understand the hardships and inconvenience it entails. Not only that, but the car ferry service cannot carry anything like the quantity of freight that is offered. A few weeks ago there were two hundred cars of freight lying on the sidings between Moncton and Tor-mentine waiting for transportation, which was not available. Perishable products, such as potatoes, have been lying in Prince Edward Island all winter and could not be moved because there was not sufficient steamship transportation, which the Dominion government promised us. Our handicaps are chiefly transportation. When we entered confederation the claim held out was that we would be given the markets of Upper Canada instead of the markets that we had developed to the south. The southern markets, of course, we came in touch with through water communication, but it was said that the Intercolonial would give us a much better market in Upper Canada, and we believed that. It did so, but the condition to-day is that while we have products which we could sell in Upper Canada, and sell to advantage at the prices obtainable in Montreal, Toronto and other cities in Upper Canada, the. transportation charges are so great that they eat up in some cases the greater part of the price we could obtain for our products before they ever reach the market. It would be a good market if we were in touch with it at a reasonable freight rate, such a freight rate as we were led to expect when we entered confederation.
We want additional transportation facilities to-day. There is a very strong agitation in Prince Edward Island for a second car ferry, for two reasons:	First, the present car ferry
is not able to perform all the service that is required there; it is not able to carry the amount of freight that is offered; second, because of the very great danger that exists today in the fact that if anything should happen to that car ferry, we should be isolated altogether. When we look back to the days when we had only ice boat communication, when a passenger leaving Prince Edward Island had to put a strap over his shoulder and assist in hauling the ice boat across, pay-
2336	COMMONS
Maritime Bights-Mr. Macdonald (Kings)
ing six dollars for the privilege, we view with alarm the prospect of something happening to that car ferry and of our having to go 'back to those conditions; because if anything does happen there will be nothing else to depend upon. In the strait of Canso, where conditions are comparatively easy compared with the strait of Northumberland, they provide a service of two car ferries; they have one auxiliary in case something should happen to the regular ferry. The distance is practically only a mile, and little ice to contend with, whereas we have nine miles, and very heavy ice to contend with; yet we have to depend on only one car ferry.
There is another way in which this government might easily help out, and that is with an air service. We could at least get mails and light baggage and perhaps some passengers, transported by air if the government would utilize their air force down there. The air force could carry on their experimenting there just as well as anywhere else, and at the same time give some reasonable service that would be of great value to Prince Edward Island by giving us a speedy and sure connection for mails, and perhaps light baggage and passengers, at all times and under all conditions. It is a serious hardship at present, at best, for passengers who have to cross by the car ferry, to be out there for hours, and days sometimes, and missing all train connections. While the service is very much better than it was many years ago, it is still far from satisfactory, and this is one of the things we expect the government to deal with.
To give an instance of the kind of service we get on that railway, I had the experience a few weeks ago of starting from Borden to Charlottetown. After getting off the car ferry several hours late, we had to get into a train, and although the authorities knew that the train had to start out from Borden, when the passengers got aboard there were no lights; something had gone wrong with the electric light apparatus, and we were furnished with old worn-out cars from the railway system on the mainland, with one lantern to light the whole coach. We had not gone very far before a brake beam gave out, and we were detained till that was repaired. We went a little further and then the air hose broke, and the braking system was out of commission. I just mention these things so that hon. gentlemen may have some idea of the difficulties we have to contend with. These things are unknown on the mainland, and the western members I am sure can hardly realize that such conditions exist; but these are some of our problems.

I do not believe a commission of this kind is good enough. I think we can present these matters to the federal government ourselves just as well as any commission could possibly do; in fact, we could do it better. Particularly I say this, that if a commission was deemed to be necessary, if the government felt they could not deal with the question satisfactorily themselves, they would have been wise to select at least one or two practical business men from the Maritime provinces as members of that commission. However, I am not criticizing the personnel of the commission. I am glad to know that a former Prince Edward Islander, Dr. Macmillan, is one of the members. I hope that he at all events will have the interests of his native province at heart, and see that some of our hardships are remedied.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House to any great extent because the general features of the question have been already discussed rather fully. But I do hope that action of some kind will foe taken, and I am sorry the government have found1 it necessary to delegate this matter to a commission, instead of dealing with it themselves at this present session. These delays are expensive, and they are costing Prince Edward Island, as well at the other Maritime provinces, much hardship and much loss. Not only that, but in addition to the loss and the hardship, a great deal of discontent has developed; it is developing day by day. The longer these conditions exist the more will that discontent grow, and the greater danger there will be that some movement will take firm hold of the people which may possibly have very serious consequences for the whole Dominion of Canada and the confederation pact. There is a real danger there, and I would like to appeal to the Prime Minister and the members of his government to deal as speedily as possible with these matters, with the particular object of allaying this discontent, which is perhaps a more serious feature of the situation than the loss and1 hardship, financial and otherwise, which the people in the Maritime' provinces are suffering.
In conclusion, referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) who has just spoken, I do not know that protection enters into this question to any great extent, but so far as the members from the Maritime provinces are concerned, there is no question whatever where they stand on the principle of protection. They were all elected on that principle, and they represent that principle, believing it is the best thing for the interests of Canada as a whole. When the hon. member speaks about the delegation

Maritime Rights-Mr. MacNutt
that came from the Maritime provinces four years ago, and says that they had diametrically opposite views, I would ask him why did they not carry their views into effect in this parliament when they had the power to do it. I would once again plead with the government for action, and speedy action, in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take up but a short time in speaking to this resolution, for there is very little I can add to what I said on this question on a previous occasion, and repetition would be merely a waste of the valuable time of this parliament. I think it was the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) who declared that the question of Maritime rights would be presented at every available opportunity throughout this session. In view of that declaration I make no apology for addressing the House to-night
I w'as somewhat amused at the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) who ventured the opinion that no contractual rights had been taken away from us. I warn the hon. gentleman that in expressing such an opinion he is venturing on very thin ice. Would my hon. friend have us believe that the pledges of the Fathers of Confederation are no more sacred than the promises of a horse trader? I can assure my hon. friend that if the Maritime rights commission, which is shortly expected to function, entertains the same ideas with regard to the spirit of the confederation pact, that, commission will be very short-lived indeed, in fact its dissolution will begin the very first day it meets. Why, Mr. Speaker, the whole crux of the situation depends upon whether we are going to honour the pledges that were entered into at the time of confederation. It was upon the strength of those pledges and those pledges alone that the representatives of the Maritime provinces agreed to the pact. As I Stated here on a previous occasion, the mere laying of two streaks of steel from Moncton to Quebec through a wilderness of 500 miles was not a sufficiently powerful thing of itself to induce the brainy men of those days who acted for the Maritime provinces to subscribe to confederation. We did not want to enter into confederation; we were persuaded to do so by the pledges given at that time. And the commission which is charged with making the investigation into Maritime province rights must acknowledge that those pledges are equally as binding as section 145 of the British North America Act, which was read by the Minister of National Defence this afternoon.
Unless that is done we shall never arrive at a real solution of our troubles in the Mari-times.
We have been told on several occasions during the present session that in advocating Maritime rights we were raising a sectional cry. In this I do not agree. It is the duty of every member in this House to see that the interests of the district which he represents are carefully safeguarded; and surely hon. gentlemen to my left will resent the idea that in advocating the building of the Hudson Bay railway, and other large enterprises, they are laying themselves open to the charge of raising the sectional cry. I believe that if the representatives from the respective constituencies, or provinces, do not look after the rights of those portions of Canada, they cannot expect members from other parts of the Dominion to do it for them.
A few days ago the legislature of Nova Scotia passed a resolution on this subject. That resolution is brief and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read it. It is worded as follows:
Whereas Nova Scotia in entering confederation made possible the unification end consolidation of a British dominion on this continent;
And whereas at that time certain pledges were given that such measures would be undertaken and such policies pursued as would ensure for the future a satisfactory economic position for this province;
And whereas the pledges given have been disregarded as a result of which Nova Scotia has not shared in equal measure in the prosperity enjoyed by the Dominion as a whole;
And whereas the government is now engaged in preparing a memorandum setting forth in detail the claims of the province with the object in view of seeking such adequate redress as will ensure such a return of contentment and prosperity to our people;
Therefore be it resolved that this House approves the action now being taken by this government,
And be it further resolved that sueh memorandum be presented by the government to the federal government with the assurance that the people of this province believe that adequate remedies exist and must be applied.
The foregoing resolution passed the legislature on a strict party vote, the three Liberal members of the House voting against it. That resolution was not presented in any party spirit or with any desire to make party capital. Premier Rhodes closed a memorable address with which he supported the resolution in the following words:
The serpent of secession has raised its slimy head in this province, so I am told. I wish to dissociate myself with any man who ever suggests secession. There are those who say we would have been better off had we not entered confederation. From the bottom of my heart I think we were wise to have entered confederation. I believe the Fathers of Confederation built better than they knew. They were men of prophetic vision, and that we have not reaped the full benefit

2338	COMMONS
Maritime Rights-Mr. MacNutt
of confederation is due more to neglect on our part, and I say regardless of whether a Conservative or Liberal government was in power at Ottawa, that the remedies for our ills can be found within the four corners of confederation. If we will only diligently seek them and apply them we will solve our problems.
Like Premier Rhodes I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we can solve our problems not only within the four corners of confederation but within the four walls of this building. I believe the representatives from the Maritime provinces have sufficient data to enable this investigation to be carried on while this House is in session. I think it was the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who made the suggestion a short time ago that a parliamentary committee be named here before whom the desired investigation could be held. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) characterized the suggestion as a good one and expressed the belief that the government was ready to consider such an appointment. Unfortunately, following that announcement the minister was taken to the hospital a very sick man and for some weeks he was absent from the deliberations of the government. I believe, Sir, that if the hon. minister, who is the only minister from the Maritime provinces, had been in the councils of the government during those weeks, a parliamentary committee would have been appointed rather than the royal commission which has been named by the government. We are glad indeed to hear his voice in the House this afternoon, and we hope he may yet prevail upon the government to name a parliamentary committee before whom we may take our case. The question is such an important one that it seems to me unsafe to allow it to be dealt with by a royal commission for the next six, eight or twelve months. We realize that the situation is a very difficult one for any government, and personally I sympathize with the government which has to face the problem. I believe it is the biggest problem that has had to be dealt with by any government in recent years. But it must be faced, and the sooner it is faced the better for this country and I am sure the better for the Maritime provinces.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) a few moments ago referred to the west not getting more than the east. I should like to draw his attention to the matter of the distribution of outlay. This information can be obtained from the reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Railways and Canals. I think I might present that to the hon. member at some future time, but not to-night. As the transportation question in Canada seems to transcend all other questions, I have recently secured1 a copy of an address given by D. A. McGibbon, Professor of political economy in the University of Alberta. This address was delivered before the agricultural society in Saskatoon on January 14, 1926. I have not the pleasure of an acquaintance with' the professor. I do not know whether he is a Maritime province man or not, but in his address he told the people that logically and morally he believed the position of the people of the Maritimes was absolutely unattackable. He referred to four great transportation problems; first the demands of British Columbia that the railway should make very low rates to enable that province to handle all the grain of Alberta and western Saskatchewan; second, the agitation for the completion for the Hudson Bay route as a grain carrying channel; third, the project of

Maritime Rights-Mr. MaeNutt
deepening the St. Lawrence to enable ocean going carriers to load at Fort William and Port Arthur, and fourth, the contention of the Maritime provinces that the people of Halifax and St. John should handle the Canadian grain that now goes out via New York, Baltimore and Philadelphia. I regret that this pamphlet is so long, because I would like to see it in the hands of every hon. member in this House who has not seen it. I will quote briefly a few portions of it. He says:
The facts that I have placed before you suggest a conclusion which may not have occurred to you. All these projects, in so far as they lean upon the government, in so far as they aim to divert trade, industry and capital from the courses they would naturally take under conditions of free enterprise, are part and parcel of a policy of protection. Many people in Canada identify protection only in connection with the policy of maintaining a protective tariff. But that is a mistake. A protective tariff operates to divert capital and industry into lines that it would not take if the government had not intervened. This is what all these transportation measures, directly or indirectly, propose to do. The bringing of transportation systems within the scope of economic protectionism is well known to students of the subject. The German authority Grunzel points out that in Germany before the war, "railway rates became not merely an auxiliary to protective duties, but in a still higher degree a means of encouraging exportations". The Germans manipulated railways rates to feed their own ports at the expense of their Belgian and French and Dutch competitors. Grunzel relates how Bismark exerted his influence upon the railways to make them "become instruments of government policy."
Of exactly similar import are the reductions arranged for on coal from Alberta to Ontario. The government has granted a sum of money drawn from the taxpayers of Canada to make these shipments possible. This sum of money is a bounty expended in the interests of encouraging home industry. The same thing is true of the government subsidizes a route to Europe via Hudson Bay, or a ship canal via the St. Lawrence, or by meeting deficits on the National Railways, due to its requiring them to carry grain exports at less than remunerative rates.
Then he proceeds:
The claims of the Maritimes.
This brings me to the complaints that are being registered by the cities of St. John and Halifax. Logically and morally, I believe their position is absolutely unattackable.
I will repeat that and emphasize it.
Logically and morally I believe their position is absolutely unattackable. Transportation ventures, all purporting to be fer the national benefit, are being or have been subsidized right and left by our national government. On the basis of political promises, on the ground of transportation subsidies given elsewhere, in the very words setting forth the reasons for the construction of what are now the National railways, our sister provinces by the sea and the city of Quebec have the right to feel that their claims have not received full consideration. The promises which the people of Canada endorsed by the election of 1904 have not been implemented. . .
Nor can I agree with a former premier of Nova Scotia when he said that the grain growers of the 14011-149J
west should ship their grain through Canadian Atlantic seaboard ports even though it cost them money to do so. That is too much to expect of human nature, nor is it in accord with the logic of economic protectionism, of which all these transportation ventures and schemes are a type.
This leads only to one conclusion. We cannot expect the Board of Railway Commissioners to order the railways to make rates that the latter can show are not remunerative in order to subsidize Canadian routes. Valuable as its function is, there are metes and bounds to what it can accomplish. The only way by which a volume of grain shipments might be set flowing to. Canadian Atlantic seaboard ports is through parliament, frankly subsidizing the route. The method of ac

complishment would be: (1) to have the Board of Railway Commissioners make a thorough investigation and' determine a rate that would not cause loss to the railways; (2) determine at what rates grain should reach tidewater in order to compete with the American range of ports; (3) the difference between these two figures-would have to be made up by a rebate to the exporter using Canadian lines and seaports; (4) the burden of making these rebates would have to fall upon the Dominion treasury; (5) such rates should come into effect with the closing of the St. Lawrence river, and should remain available each year until the opening of that channel in the spring. This is the only method I know of by which the Maritime seaports may hope to share in a large way in the export of Canadian grain.
If the people of Canada wish to utilize their own ports this is the course they will have to pursue. Economic protectionism has been part of the policy of Canada for 46 years. The doctrine of the development through protection of infant industries has been preached incessantly-a subsidy to encourage the Maritime ports would be in accord with the logic of that policy.
I should like also to refer to a paper that came into my hands a few days ago. Hon. members can see it. There is this heading in two-inch, heavy type, block letters in the Boston Advertiser of March 31, 1926:
Secession Move in Maritimes
Separatist banner is likely to be hoisted on birthday of confederation.
The 59th birthday of Canada's confederation, on July 1, next, may see the banner of secession formally hoisted by the Maritimes provinces, if plans now afoot here mature according to schedule.
Secession rumours have stirred eastern Canada before now, and the issue of "Maritime rights" has been one of those most persistently to the fore in the present session of parliament. The movement now launched, according to its sponsors, is designed to fan the embers of unrest into an open flame, and to win complete fiscal autonomy for the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Geographic transportation conditions make it impossible for them to find a market for their exports in the other provinces of Canada and the present United States tariff closes the doors of that country to their produce.
Other planks in the secessionist platform are:
Complete control of the provinces' natural resources.
Provincial collections of all duties and excise, income taxes and other levies.	[DOT]
Control of all fisheries within the provinces.
Co-operation with the Dominion in military defence, postal services and navigation.
Contributions to the National railway deficit to be in proportion to mileage in the province.

Maritime Rights-Mr. MacNutt
Contributions to the national debt to be in proportion to population.
Appointment of a royal commission to investigate the *grievances of the Martime provinces, was one of the promises made by Premier King at the opening of the present session of the Dominion parliament. But the secessionists declare that their grievances have been too long ignored; that the hour for investigation and negotiation has passed, and the hour for direct action has struck.
That is what is appearing in papers across the line. I am not a secessionist. I do not like the word. I do not believe that at present you can find a great number of secessionists in my province, but I believe we are to-day standing upon a volcano of public feeling in that province, a volcano which is liable to burst into eruption at any time. I plead with this government and ask that they recede from their present position in the appointment of a royal commission, act upon the suggestion of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and name a parliamentary committee before whom we can place the case for the Maritime provinces.

speechtext:
Maritime Rights-Mr. Church
this folly of free trade, look at what it has done for the natural resources of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. For almost fifty years the natural resources of Nova Scotia were administered according to the principles of Adam Smith, as those principles were interpreted by corporations, corporationist Liberals, in Halifax with headquarters in Montreal. Private ownership grabbed all the water powers and coal resources in sight.
I believe our national railway system might be so operated as to help very considerably to solve the problems of the Maritimes. Is it to be operated for the benefit of the people that own the railway, or for the benefit of the American coal barons who have their headquarters in Philadelphia? A committee of this House dealt with the coal question and found that 17 a ton was a fair rate for Alberta and Nova Scotia coal. What happened? Nothing was done. Sir Henry Thornton after accepting it in two years openly repudiated the finding of the committee. He might as well have quoted a rate $15 or $25 a ton as $9, because anything over $7 is prohibitive and, as I contend, is a surrender to the American coal barons of the coaj market of the central provinces and is a blow to the coal industry of Alberta and the Maritime provinces.
I believe in a national policy for the solution of all our problems. We mobilized our resources in war time with great advantage; it is equally necessary and advantageous to mobilize them in times of peace. We should mobilize our railways in peace time to develop our great natural resources. If that was done you would have the national railway system co-operating in the solution of these maritime problems. I entered the lists on behalf of the Maritime provinces with a fuel policy at my first session of parliament. I have never yet seen any reason to regret that action. I have advocated a national policy for the marketing of our coal, our grain, our fruit, and all our products. I support that policy to-day after a very close study of conditions in the Maritime provinces, which I had the good fortune to visit for a couple of brief periods
10 p.m. during the war. I then reached the conclusion that there were never three provinces where Providence has done so much and man so little. In my opinion, protection for the Maritime provinces is not a luxury, it is a necessity.
Our railways are Americanized to-day. Canadian grain is carried at preferential rates to the head of the lakes, where it is diverted to the port of Buffalo, although we have

spent millions of dollars on our canal system in an endeavour to secure an all-Canadian route. Buffalo to-day has the cream of the milling business, not only of the United States but of Canada as well. We are losing that whole industry. The grain industry is not a north-and-south industry, as some hon. gentlemen to my left contend, but an east-and-west industry, and an overseas industry, with the product selling in the markets of continental Europe. I went into this question at length last session and discussed the elevator combine, the transportation combine, and the Great Lakes combine. There is now a merger of all Canadian and American boats on the Great Lakes, and the result is that our grain trade is being diverted to Buffalo, as a return that was brought down to the House on the 3rd of March last shows. If you take 150 as the unit, 100 per cent of our grain goes through United States ports, and only 50 through Canadian channels. I think that is a fair summary of the return that was brought down. The grain industry is one which could do a great deal for the Maritime provinces. In Ontario we used to have a chain of elevators in days gone by, but to-day there is hardly a terminal elevator in the whole of central Ontario. Why? Buffalo a few years ago had only a few elevators, but the whole elevator policy and grain policy of this country has resulted in the erection of twenty-eight big elevators in Buffalo to handle Canadian grain, as is set out in the report of the grain commission and has resulted in the great bulk of our grain going through American ports. The more you look into this thing the more clearly you see how the Maritime provinces have got the worst of it all along the line, through our grain not being routed through Canadian channels. Sir Henry Thornton has made somewhat of a superficial study of the question, and his conclusions are contrary to those of the grain commission which studied this particular problem. If there is any industry in this country which should be under a national policy, it is the grain-growing industry. The United States is a grain-growing country; it grows far more than it can consume itself; it consumes only little more than half of its crop and has an exportable surplus of about a third of its crop. We consume a little more than that, and it is the price obtained for the exportable surplus which by the economic law of supply and demand determines the price for the part used at home. What has been the result in Canada? Canada's grain crop should go through Canadian ports under adequate protection

Maritime Rights-Mr. Church
and by Canadian railways. Buffalo has twenty-eight elevators to-day as a result of the folly of such an anti-Canadian grain policy. The industrial department of the city of Buffalo, in its advertising, speaks of the great boon the present grain policy of Canada regarding grain has been to that port. It has built up the port of Buffalo, and built up traffic on the Erie barge canal. Instead of our grain going to Port Colborne and then to Montreal, it goes to Buffalo and New York and Baltimore, where in violation of the law and by a bootlegging policy it is mixed with American cheap grain and milled, whence it goes out in the form of flour, under certificate, to Europe as No. 1 grade. The United States has captured not only the oversea grain trade of Canada, but the oversea market for the milling trade as well, and the solution of this grain and milling problem and the development of the industry on an embargo principle in this country would pay off the deficit we have on the National railways of fifty to sixty million dollars a year. The Buffalo papers for the past few months have carried columns of printed matter wondering if at this session anything was going to be done to divert Canadian grain through Canadian channels by placing an embargo on hard wheat as recommended by the grain commission. According to a report of the American Shipping Board published in the Toronto Globe this morning, about 25 per cent less grain is now going through United States channels than last year. That has been diverted to Canadian channels as a result of the educational campaign that has been conducted in this House in the matter of a grain embargo during the last four sessions. Secondly, it has been due to the invasion of new blood, the sixteen new members in this. House from the Maritime provinces.
The coal problem is also connected with this question. Coal should be carried on the same preferential rates as grain and flour, for after all is said and done, coal is equivalent to food, because nothing on the breakfast table can be prepared as food without the use of coal. You can do without a meal, once in a while but you cannot do without fuel in winter time; we have to burn coal for six or seven months in the year. I have proposed to this House that we should have a national policy on coal, and that the government merchant marine and the National railways should be mobilized and utilized to put this policy into effect. Nova Scotia had a Liberal government for thirty-four years, but did you ever hear of the legislature of Nova
Scotia making any attempt to solve this coal problem until the new government came in? Did they send any delegation here last year when the Conservatives brought this matter up? Premier Armstrong prepared a learned memorandum in which he spoke of the evils of this particular problem. I would urge that a system of bonuses, subsidies and subventions, be applied to the coal industry. We have the president of the Canadian National Railwaj'S, and its dummy board meets now and then; it looks to me more like the board of a Liberal campaign fund than a board of railway directors. Some of them do not know any more about running a railway than they do about running a movie theater. The people of Canada are disappointed in the management of the National railways to-day. We have spent nearly two billion dollars on the National railway system to help solve our problem, and we are disappointed with the result.
Where does the railway commission stand to-day? I have not heard of them. They are supposed to investigate freight rates as applied to Maritime rights of their own volition. The Railway Act requires them to prevent unjust, unfair, and undue discrimination between localities, and lays down the principle that there shall be equality of treatment, that preference shall not be given to one product at the expense of another. A railway must be operated to provide, first, sinking fund and fixed charges on the investment; secondly, it must make operating expenses; thirdly, a reasonable dividend on the investment; fourthly, provide, if possible, a sum for betterments and extensions. The basis of all rate structures in this country is the Crowsnest pass agreement. Who is responsible for that bungle? The Liberal party. Who is responsible for building the Grand Trunk Pacific, and for the deficits on the National railways? Who is responsible for building the National Transcontinental, when one transcontinental with a double track would have been sufficient for our needs? The Liberal party. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, a man for whom we have the utmost respect, went up and down the Maritime provinces during that National Transcontinental campaign and promised that grain would be routed through Canadian channels and that the Maritime provinces would come into their own when that railway was built. What happened? I venture to say that we would not have had the railway bungle we have in this country to-day if Sir William Mulock and the late Mr. J. F. Lister had had their way. They attacked the Laurier-Sifton

Maritime Rights-Mr. Church
proposals for the construction of the Crowsnest pass railway. Sir John Willison for weeks and months carried the slogan across the front page of the Globe, "Concessions for Concessions," representing the maximum rates proposed in the Crowsnest pass contract as then, in 1897, and forever applicable to shipments from every point on the Canadian Pacific system in Canada. The Crowsnest pass deal was put through by the Liberal party and from that day forward freight rates were fixed by statute, preferences given, and a political rate structure established. The enactment of that legislation was the greatest mistake this country ever made. It is responsible to-day for a great many of the transportation ills from which this country is suffering. It is the basis of the political railway rate structure of Canada from coast to coast. We have always had a political railway rate structure in this country. We have not yet, and never have had, an economic rate structure. The railway commission is not competent to create an economic rate structure because this parliament has seen fit, since the inception of the Crowsnest pass agreement, to fix rates on some products and not on others, and establish certain tolls by legislation at the expense of others, for 'instance on grain and flour from the west to the head of the lakes. Who pays for this? The central provinces of Canada. The railway commission is not in a position to-day to solve this problem as long as the Crowsnest pass legislation, or any part of it, remains in force with all the evils flowing therefrom. I believe this unfair legislation is one of the reasons why the Maritime provinces are suffering from the discrimination pointed out by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley). I have copies of the railwa3r tariffs and codes which have been passed for the last ten years and I can corroborate every word the hon. gentleman has said not only as regards the rates on steel and coal but also as regards those on fruit, lumber and .agricultural, and other commodities carried between the head of the lakes and the city of Sydney, between the head of the lakes and Halifax, between Hamilton and Montreal, and between Hamilton and the seaboard. Between these points the greatest discrimination exists.
Instead of having a proper regulation of rates and a fair rate established as between one city and another, certain basic products have been selected for a preference which has been given certain parts of Canada at the expense of the rest of the Dominion. Not only has the hon. member for Pictou spoken

in an absolutely correct manner, but the statements made by the representatives for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) and Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short) are entirely accurate. Reasonable and equitable rates are necessary in the interest of the great fishing industry of the Maritime provinces, as well as other industries, but instead the worst discrimination exists.
A proper solution of this rate problem would bring the producer and the consumer together in a mutually satisfactory manner, and meet the existing difficulties in a variety of ways. The province of Ontario has by cheap light and power solved its problems by protection in a very satisfactory manner. For thirty-four years the needs of the situation in the matter of cheap light and power were overlooked bj^ the various provincial Liberal governments there, but the Liberal party could see nothing and had no vision in Ontario. It remained for the government of the late Sir James P. Whitney and the late Sir Adam Beck to take action and they handled the situation in a manner which has made Ontario the admiration of the world. The following are some of the results which have been achieved by the hydro in Ontario:
1.	Every dollar of the $160,000,000 Hydro investment is earning interest and sinking fund.
2.	Hydro investment saved Ontario from a coal famine that would have bankrupted the province in war time.
3.	Hydro investment saved 2,200,000 shareholders over $75,000,000 in reduced coal, light and power bills.
4.	Hydro investment saved Ontario over $100,000,000, on coal prices which would have gone to $30 per ton in war time but for the Hydro investment that gave Ontario the equivalent of 3,000,000 tons of United States coal per annum.
If Ontario can solve its problems through the Hydro-Electric Commission why cannot the Maritime provinces do the same? The hydro-electric policy involves the protectionist principle. It is protection in the truest sense; it means utilizing the public resources of a province for the benefit of that province. The hydro has fought in Ontario the battle of the masses against the classes. If the principle involved in the policy of the HydroElectric Commission of Ontario in the conservation of its light and power resources had been applied to the Maritime provinces, those provinces would have developed their coal mines, power, and timber instead of giving those resources away to political favourites. I say to hon. gentlemen from the Maritime provinces: Do not blame everything on the central provinces of the Dominion, do not blame everything on the confederation pact. The people of Nova Scotia kept in power for thirty-four years a Liberal administration that

Maritime Rights-Mr. Church
gave away its resources to be developed for private greed and private gain. The Maritime provinces would have had a place in the sun long ago if the people had looked after their resources and conserved them. If the principle of protection were applied to the development of the power, coal, fisheries and lumber resources of the Maritime provinces it would solve the existing problems almost automatically. After all Providence only helps those who help themselves. The people of those provinces have only themselves to blame for not working out the solution of their problems on the protective principle and in the manner I have indicated.
I wish now to say a word or two about the way in which the Canadian National Railways have been Americanized. The passenger and to some extent the freight rates from St. Louis and Chicago, and points beyond that as far as Minneapolis, to Montreal, are only about one-third of the rates from Toronto, Hamilton and London to the same port. In other words, under the auspices of this parliament, and of the board of management of the system, the Canadian National Railways are being operated for the benefit of foreigners at Rotterdam and other cities in Europe and America and for the benefit of cities and towns in the United States. Sir Henry Thornton would rather quote a price like $9, $10 or $15 a ton for the carriage of Canadian coal, in order to permit the Philadelphia coal barons to get the cream of the business, than quote a rate of $7 in the case of Alberta coal and $4 in the case of coal from the Maritime provinces and solve some of confederation's problems. If the latter policy were pursued, Alberta and the Maritime provinces would get the cream of the Canadian coal business rather than the American coal barons.
In addition to that, the L'nited States branch lines of the Canadian National railways are being operated in such a way as to divert trade to Portland and other American ports. The Canadian shippers are not to blame. They must obey the railway laws of this country. That those laws are what they are to-day is the fault of the present and past Canadian parliaments, and the parliament that preceded the present one, in erecting in Canada a political rate structure instead of an economic rate structure. We believed in mobilizing the resources of our railways and transportation systems in time of war. Why do we not do the same in peace time? Surely we should do that in order to protect our industries,, our people and our markets from foreign competitors. Why was an elevator built at Halifax if there was no grain to put
in it? Why have we spent about 2 billion dollars in building railways for the benefit of the United States, the highest protected country in the world? The condition in the Maritime provinces is very largely due to the fact that they have not had a safeguarding of industries act, and consequently their industries have not been properly protected. If they had had a Stanley Baldwin in the Maritime provinces during the thirty-four years of Liberal administration, he would have accomplished something for the provinces and would have done a great deal to protect their resources and their products. The Maritimes want an economic revival and a revivalist to lead it. What the Maritime provinces require is an act for the safeguarding of industries and protection. But what has happened? Instead of this government attempting to solve the problem in a rational way they have made a football of it. I do not know what this Maritime commission has been appointed for. What is the commission to do? To find out what the Maritime rights are? The members of the government can easily ascertain what those rights are if they read the speeches of hon. members from those provinces on this side of the House.
The former Premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Armstrong, seemed to find out very suddenly what Maritime rights were. He came up to Ottawa previous to the election and found out what the Maritime rights were, and he presented his bill of rights. He refers to the question of coal, steel, fisheries, lumbering and all the other matters relating to the provinces. If I understood the reports in the papers, he was told that the government of Canada did not understand what Maritime rights were. I think however, they have had a better idea of those rights since the 29th of October.
I believe the provinces of central Canada desire to trade with the Maritimes, and they think it would be much -better for confederation if they would. The quicker the railway commission, of their own volition, settle these problems for the Maritime provinces, the better for -Canada. That would be far better than waiting for this government to take action. The career of some of the Liberal prime -ministers and statesmen who came from the Maritime provinces to this House after having enjoyed cabinet rank in the provincial legislatures, is not reassuring. They have made a great success, perhaps, in finding material for speeches and in delivering speeches, but they have been about the biggest public failures in Canada when it came to doing anything in the way of practical policies

Maritime Rights-Mr. Church
for the Maritime provinces. I have seen them administering the affairs of the Maritime provinces, and they have treated the resources of the Maritime provinces as they would a Christmas tree; and made handouts off the Christmas tree-to all the big interests. Of course, they took the coal resources off the Christmas tree and grabbed many other things, such as power, timber resources and water-powers. They played Santa Claus for 34 years to the resources of the Maritime provinces, the timber wealth and the fisheries, and in fact I might say the products of the sea, the soil, the forests and the mines were given away in hand-outs. They handed these resources to whom? To a commission on public utilities? No, they handed them over to the big interests and party favourites. They transferred many of these interests to Montreal, and the big interests took charge of them there. These Liberal provincial premiers Ottawa bound-abound in public speech, but as a result of their work for forty years in the provinces, those provinces are not a dollar richer or have an additional inhabitant. They have been ruled for thirty-four years by a sort of non-apostolic succession of rulers and premiers and now that apostolic succession of Liberal rulers has been displaced. They believed they could make Nova Scotia rich by the free and unrestricted distribution of the coal, the power and other resources of the province to favourites and by giving preferences. They did and they were mistaken. They have handed out all these resources to the big interests in Montreal at the expense of the Maritimes. They have carried on this principle of handing out these resources, not only the coal but the other valuable assets; even the banking system-everything-has been sacrificed for the big interests. Talk about banking! Who is responsible for the bank legislation? Two or three of the finance ministers came from the Maritimes. What did they do? They allowed the solicitors of the Bankers association to draft the Bank Act and as drawn up it was never enforced or carried out. You cannot blame central Canada for that. Blame your own statesmen who could prepare and make speeches but could not create a policy for their province. We have had many mergers of banks, and we have seen the actions of those big interest companies which had control of the coal and other Maritime industries. They have had coal strikes, lockouts and other calamities as a result. Talk about agriculture 1 What did the Liberal Premiers of Nova Scotia ever do down in those provinces for agriculture or lumbering?

What was done in the last parliament in the way of bill of rights? Nothing that I know of. We have had a debate annually in this chamber for three years in regard to the national coal supply. Did we ever get any help from the Premier of Nova Scotia or from any of his ministers in regard to the coal question? No resolution was ever sent here to help us along.
I am glad this question has come up. While we have many problems in Ontario, we are getting practically no help in the wray of a tariff-all is nibbling and reducing and uncertainty of tariffs. We have had a very uncertain tariff for the last few years, and we have had a reduction of the tariff which has had the result of closing many industries. Ontario is badly in need of protection for its basic products and industries. We could very well present a bill of rights from Ontario. I do not know of any province which is suffering more on account of the transportation problem than Ontario. They thlk about Ontario getting the Grand Trunk Pacific. They did not want it. The province of Ontario had to build the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway themselves, and this was a work for the general advantage of Canada. They will have to build their own railway to James Bay. Ontario did not want the duplication of three National Transcontinental or three or four lines also Toronto to Belleville where one line with a double track would have been sufficient.
Sir William Mulock and other prominent men opposed the system of Crowsnest railway construction which produced railway chaos in rates. I approach this question with a feeling of sympathy with the Maritime provinces. What would Canada have done in time of war, were it not for the Intercolonial? It was all right to have a national railway to the Maritime provinces in time of war, to transport manufactures and goods to the seaboard. But when the war was over they soon forgot all about it. During the war the people were glad to have the British fleet to protect our shores and our Maritime ports, but as soon as the war was over they were glad to forget all about it and do nothing to contribute for all this protection and Maritime freedom.
The solution of this problem is not by means of a commission. I have lost confidence in any commission appointed by the government. We have not got responsible government in this country to-day. Problem after problem is side-stepped and handed over to commissions. I never knew a commission in Canada yet to accomplish anything, except one, and that was the commission which solved the light and power problem of Ontario and

Maritime Rights-Mr. Mackenzie King
created a surplus for every municipality. I refer to the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario. The railway commission got lost during the last two or three years. They were appointed to fix rates, and they have had the cases of the Bell Telephone and the express companies and other public service corporations before them, but what did thej do? These companies come down and ask the railway commission to increase rates and presented figures to the commission. The commission practically took their figures as gospel and increased rates were allowed and granted.	They took their figures of expenditures, and so on. They might just as well have allowed the companies to make their own tolls and fares and their own rates. Instead of the railway commission having long ago solved the problem of equality of rates and preventing unjust, unfair and undue discrimination between localities and provinces, they have done nothing of their own volition to carry out the functions for which they were appointed by this honourable House.
In conclusion, I congratulate the mover of the resolution, I congratulate the Maritime provinces on having been led into a revival and on having sixteen revivalists here in parliament to waken up the people of this country and parliament to do something practical for the people of the Maritime provinces by adopting a policy of protection to remedy Maritime ills. A policy of protection for all the provinces from coast to coast is the only thing that can solve our economic ills and bring about a better understanding among the different provinces that go to make up this British confederacy of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with my friend and colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) in expressing appreciation of the attitude in which this resolution has been approached for the most part by all hon. members who have thus far spoken upon it. The debate throughout the day has been conducted largely without partisan spirit. Hon. members have recognized that the subject is one of the most important with which our country is concerned and with which parliament can be called upon to deal, and doubtless this fact has influenced the addresses which have been made in the course of the day. One is bound to feel that hon. members of the House have at heart first and foremost the interest of our great Dominion and not less a desire to show to our friends in the Maritime provinces that, in so far as we come from other provinces
in the Dominion, our attitude towards the Maritime provinces is a wholly sympathetic one.
This question of Maritime rights or of the just claims the Maritime provinces may have is not a question to be viewed from the standpoint of Conservative or Liberal, of government or of opposition. It is rather a matter between the Maritime provinces and the other provinces of the Dominion. I think the essential feature of it is that in so far as it is a question at all it is a question of the other provinces of the Dominion joining in a wholehearted way in an endeavour to have the Maritime provinces feel that, as they are a part of confederation, every effort should be made to see that their rights in confederation are implemented to the letter and in full.
If it will help at all to take this resolution out of the realm of possible partisan discussion, I should like to go one better than my hon. friend the member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) who has seconded the resolution. He said that he hoped this motion would be pressed to a vote and that the House would approve the resolution as it is drafted. I should rather hope that it will not be necessary to have a vote and that the House will express its approval unanimously of the resolution which has been moved and which he has seconded. The resolution is one which in my opinion the House should unanimously accept.
