speechtext: May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that I referred to the Canadian National Railway board, not to the railway commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
But this is an instruction from the government to the commission which has the control of railway rates and is the proper body to deal with the rate question. If the Canadian National railway is not carrying out the policy of the government in this matter, it becomes the duty of the railwajr commission, when so instructed by an order of the government, to see that that policy is carried out. A word from the commission should be much more effective than any communication from the government itself to the management of the National railways. Nothing could be more emphatic than the words "the fixed policy of the government." It is not some chance assertion of policy. Our desire is that the railway commission, the railways, in fact, everyone shall realize what the policy of the government is-namely, that we wish to encourage trade over Canadian railways east and west, and that in particular we wish to encourage Canadian trade via Canadian ports. That is the fixed policy of the government and our hope in connection with the enquiry before the railway commission and before the roya^ commission is that that policy will become more firmly emphasized, and as a consequence more effectively carried out as opportunity offers.
Now, I am not aware that the House has had before it up to the present a copy of the order in council which refers this matter specifically to the railway commission. I will therefore read it to the House. It was
approved on January 7 of this year and is in these words:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 6th January, 1926, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, representing that the Committee of the Privy Council has had under consideration the advisability of encouraging to the fullest extent the movement of Canadian grain and other products through Canadian ports.
The minister states that by order in council (P.C. 8S6), dated 5th June, 1925, the Beard of Railway Commissioners for Canada was directed to make a thorough investigation, already under way, of the rates structures of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the Dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries, and in particular to:
(a) the claim asserted on behalf of the Maritime provinces -that they are entitled to the restoration of the rate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919;
(b)	the encouragement of the movement of traffic through Canadian ports;
(c)	the increased traffic westward and eastward through Pacific coast ports owing to the expansion of trade with the Orient end to the transportation of products through the Panama Canal.
The Committee of the Privy Council therefore recommends that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada be directed, as a part of the general rate investigation above referred to, especially to enquire into the causes of Canadian grain and other products being routed or diverted to other than Canadian ports, and to take such effective notion under the Railway Act, 1919, as the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada may deem necessary to ensure, as far as possible, the routing of Canadian grain and other products through Canadian ports.
There is a statement of policy, Mr. Speaker, which is unequivocal and leaves no room for doubt. It refers to a general rate investigation, which is a larger matter that the board entered upon some time ago. As an evidence that this rate investigation is likely to be helpful to the Maritimes and is the proper way of proceeding, may I again refer to the speech from the throne which was delivered by His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor at the opening of the Nova Scotia legislature on February 9 of this year. Paragraph 12 reads as follows:
During the past summer an agreement was entered into with the governments of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to engage jointly the services of an expert to prepare a statement of facts in connection with railway freight rates affecting the Maritime prov-incse, to be submitted to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. I am informed that certain changes in rates as a result of these efforts have already effected a considerable saving to shippers in these provinces.
There is a statement made by His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor of Nova Scotia only
2352	COMMONS
Maritime Rights-Mr. Mackenzie King
a few months ago with reference to a result already achieved through representations made by a solicitor retained by 11 p.m. the Maritime provinces to appear before the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada and argue for their rights with respect to freight rates.
So, Mr. Speaker, I submit in relation to the resolution which has been moved and seconded, and which contains the reference to freight rates over the Intercolonial and their adjustment in accordance with whatever understandings there may have been at the time of and as a part of confederation, that in expecting this matter to be dealt with by the railway commission, and in particular by instructing that commission to pay special attention to this very question of routing Canadian grain and other products over Canadian railways and through Canadian ports, the government has taken the course which, if any course at all is calculated to bring about the desired result, is the one that may be expected so to do.
I might take up considerable of the time of the House by making further references to the desire and action of the government to meet the Maritime provinces with respect to matters which are of great concern to them. I would submit that this reference to the commission of certain matters is only one part of the work of the government in that regard. Last session I recall making a strong appeal to members of the Progressive party in this House to support the government in an effort to raise the tariff on bituminous slack coal, mainly because of a desire to help in the Maritime situation. I think it is permissible to refer to a debate in a previous session, though not to one in the same session, and I would like just to remind hon. members of the House of what I said at that time. This government was npt standing for any general increase of the tariff, but we were thinking of the Maritime interests with respect to a particular industry which we believed needed to be assisted in a particular way, even if the measure proposed did not accord with our policy as generally applied. I hope we shall never become such slaves to any doctrine that when we find it necessary to invoke the exception which proves the rule we shall be unwilling to make the exception. This was a case where it seemed to us there was ground for an exception, and speaking in the budget debate, on April 30th, I used the following words with reference to increasing the duty on bituminous slack coal:
We have felt further that there is one part of our Dominion which to-day has been having a hard

struggle; no one can deny that. The Maritime provinces have had and are having a hard time. We were not without hope that our action in this particular would put new faith and comfort into the hearts and minds of the people of the Maritime provinces and for no class more than those who are engaged in the hard work of mining coal in connection with the primary industries of that part of our country. We felt this was helping on as well a great national policy of selfsufficiency in the matter of our coal supplies in this country. Those were great national reasons transcending, I believe, alt other reasons. I ask my friends of the Progressive party:	Are you not going to be
magnanimous enough to sink any little feeling you may entertain with respect to some theoretical maximum on tariffs and stretch to our friends in the Maritime provinces the same helping hand they stretched out to you in good faith and good fellowship last session? You have an opportunity to do so on this budget. You have an opportunity by your action on this budget to show that in your outlook, you are something more than sectional; that, you have a broad vision; that you are thinking first of Canada as a whol$. You have your chance on this budget and it is for you to say. I again appeal to my hon. friends. It has been from this larger point of view, from the point of view of national interest as a whole, national economy, national well-being and national goodwill, that the government has taken the stand that it has on the tariff question at this particular session.
That was the attitude in which the government approached the Maritime provinces' problem at the last session of parliament, and I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that the government's attitude to-day towards the Maritime provinces is what it was then.-an attitude of seeking to understand the problem, and of seeking to meet it, of give and take as between the different provinces of this Dominion. The most unfortunate thing that could happen in this parliament is that we should begin to discuss public questions in terms of east or in terms of west. I need not remind the House of those well known lines:
But there is neither east nor west, border nor breed nor birth
When two strong men stand face to face, tho' they come from the ends of the earth!
We are sent here by our different constituencies to speak to each other as strong men, men who can speak their minds fearlessly and courageously, with one aim and one end in common, and I venture to say that if, in discussions of these questions, this House will keep first and foremost in view, the end and the aim, the idea and the ideal, which we have in common of a united Canada. we shall not have jnuch difficulty in reaching a solution of the Maritime or any other problem. That spirit I think has been evident this afternoon.
As I was saying, the government has in this matter of the commission sought to take one step which it believed was fundamental and essential to a proper understanding of and consequent dealing with the situation in

Maritime Rights-Mr. Mackenzie King
the Maritimes. Other policies we have had and have which we believe will do a lot for the Maritime provinces. I am not so sure that hon. gentlemen opposite will agree with all of them. One policy in which the Liberal party has strongly believed, and in which we still believe, is a policy of reciprocal trade in natural products. I believe that the defeat of that policy in 1911 has done more than almost any other single thing to affect adversely the situation for the Maritime provinces, for if there is one part of this Dominion that would have profited by having a wider market for the sale of the natural products, they have in such abundance, the products of the mine, of the farm, of the forest, and of the sea, it is the Maritime provinces. Our policies in that regard have had in view the well-being and the welfare of the Maritime provinces in common with the well-being and the welfare of the whole Dominion, but I would submit again that, taking the Dominion as a whole, there is no part unless it be western Canada, that would have stood to gain as much as would the Maritime provinces had that particular agreement gone into force.
But it has not been only in that particular that the government sought to further the interests of the Maritime provinces. Reference has been made several times to my having asked the question in the Maritime provinces during the last campaign, what are Maritime rights? I did ask that question, but I asked it in order to answer it, and I did answer it. My hon. friends have not done me the justice to give the answer I made at that time. Having asked the question. I proceeded to answer it by pointing out what I thought were Maritime rights, and among the things I pointed out as Maritime rights was their right to the largest possible market that could be found for their commodities; the right to have their instruments of production in the basic industries made as cheap as possible; the right to expand their trade in different directions; the right to have as much Canadian import and export trade brought through the Maritime provinces as it was possible to bring; the right to more effective steamship services as between the different parts of the Maritimes and as between the Maritimes and the British West Indies. These are only some of the answers I gave to that question. I asked the question, what are Maritime rights? But I asked it with a view to making an answer, and hon. gentlemen will find that to be the case if they care and will take the trouble to look at the speeches I made in the Maritime provinces.
May I say with regard to this question of meeting the Maritime provinces' problem, that other of our policies have had in view Maritime interests, as well as those pertaining to trade-the policy, for instance, that we had with respect to the reduction of duties on the implements of production. There was a policy intended for all of Canada, but it was a policy with very particular benefits and with particular relation to the Maritime provinces. Only last session we further reduced certain duties on some of the equipment used by fishermen, on gasoline engines installed in fishing craft, as I recall it. We had in a previous session made other reductions in the duties on the implements of production, in mining, fishing, lumbering, and agriculture, all of which were greatly to the benefit of the Maritime provinces, not exclusively, but in common with the rest of the Dominion.
In regard to the encouragement of trade through Maritime ports, in 1923, I think it was, in order to further Canadian trade by Canadian ports, we gave an additional ten per cent discount on the tariff inposed on commodities coming under the British preference into Canada where they came through Canadian ports; in other words, we increased the preference where goods coming from Great Britain or other parts of the empire enjoying the preference came through Canadian ports.
Hon. members will recall that at the inception of this movement on behalf of Maritime rights, a delegation of very considerable proportions came to Ottawa from the Maritime provinces to urge upon the government the desirability and the necessity of taking some action which would cause all trade under the British preference to come via Canadian ports, in order that the Maritimes might get the benefit of that trade. These gentlemen were no sooner assembled here than they discovered, some of them much to their chagrin, that what they had come all the way to ask for had already under the policy of this government been carried out, and that as the result of the ten per cent discount on the existing preferential rate which the government had granted, something like 98 or 99 and a fraction per cent of the total trade enjoying the British preference was coming to Canada via Canadian ports in so far as it came through ports on the Atlantic. Now, if it will cause our friends in the Maritime provinces to feel any greater trust in the government's desire to further Maritime interests by having it understood that in order to enjoy the British preference at all the trade must come through Canadian ports, I for one would be very pleased to see that

2354	COMMON'S
Maritime Rights-Mr. Mackenzie King
policy carried out-. It. might help to give more general satisfaction were the British preference made applicable only to commodities coming into Canada via Canadian ports. That, as I have said, is practically accomplished to-day by the additional discount, but if the extension of the idea by express terms will help in any way, I believe we should undertake to see that that further step is taken.
Now, to come to another matter of policy. One hon. gentleman speaking this afternoon said, "Drop the question of commissions and get down to practical business."

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mi . MACKENZIE KING: My hon. friend says Hear, hear." Well, we got down to practical business when we negotiated the trade treaty with the West Indies. True enough that treaty may mean something by way of subsidies to provide the necessary transportation facilities that will be required, we may have to ask our friends opposite to join with us in agreeing to ipay out of the public treasury a little more for subsidies in order to secure the improved steamship service which is proposed in order to get for the people of the Maritime provinces the increase in their trade we desire to see. At any rate the government has felt that one of the needs of the Maritimes was to secure for the Maritimes the nearest available market beyond our borders. Now there is a natural market for them in the West India islands, a market which if it was ever'intended to serve any purpose seems designed to suit the needs of the Maritime provinces. While the actual location of the British West Indies is closer to parts of the United States than it is to this Dominion, we have a relationship to those islands much closer in the true sense of the word than that which geography affords. We have the relationship of common kinship under a common sovereign and under a common flag. We are of the opinion that the most should be made of that relationship, and that we should seek, so far as is possible, to develop inter-*imperial trade wherever the opportunity presents itself. Here it presents itself in a very special and helpful way, in a way particularly helpful to our friends in the Maritime provinces. The government went to a good deal of trouble in the matter of negotiating that agreement. 'We did not go at it in any hurried slapdash fashion. We had a representative of this parliament visit the British West Indies. Mr. Hance Logan, the then member for Cumberland, was the gentleman
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
chosen. He had given the subject much careful study and had brought it to the attention of parliament. He visited the West Indies and extended to those islands a formal invitation to send representatives to Ottawa to meet with the representatives of the Canadian government and see if we could not work out a trade arrangement which would give to the products of the Maritimes a wider market, and to the consumers of the Maritimes as well as the consumers of other parts of Canada at a lower cost certain commodities which are produced in tropical regions and which are not produced here, though in considerable use. After a period of negotiation an agreement was come to which is before the House at the present time. Now, I believe hon. gentlemen opposite, in fact hon. gentlemen generally, are going to meet the government in the matter of permitting that agreement to go into force. Whatever criticism there may be of details, I believe the House will rise to the point of saying, "After all, here is an agreement which means something in inter-imperial relations. We are going to see it through, and we are going to give it a trial." I submit that regardless of what it may mean in the matter of a little additional cost for the establishment of proper transportation facilities it is the duty of all who have the interests of the Maritime provinces at heart to join with the government and to strengthen our hands in making that arrangement effective.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope I have not taken up too much time. My desire has been simply to point out that in this matter we have endeavoured sincerely to meet a serious condition and one which it is the supreme duty of both government and parliament to meet.
A word has been used in the course of this debate, not in any direct way but indirectly, the word "secession." I do not think it is necessary to bring that word into our discussions in this House. In this case the word was quoted from some American publication. I hear a good deal of talk about going to the United States for this purpose and for that, but I do not think we need to go to the United States in order to bring into this House any talk about secession in the Dominion. We can afford to leave that word out of our vocabulary altogether. But do not let me be misunderstood. I do believe that in the Maritime provinces there is a feeling of unrest. I do believe that in the Maritime provinces there is a feeling that they have suffered in sorqe particulars. I do not believe that feeling will be removed by ignoring the situation. Neither do I believe that the
235C

Maritime Rights-Mr. Mcighen
situation will be helped by seeking to secure in virtue of it party advantage or party gain in any particular. If we study the history of this continent we will find that the experience of the Maritime provinces, whether they were in or out of confederation, was bound to a certain extent to have been very much what it has been for the simple reason that as the great west developed, as expansion has gone westward, the older provinces of the Dominion were bound to suffer considerably with respect to their agricultural and some of their other industries. It was so in the New England states, it has been so in every country; where there has been expansion and development from old settled parts to new, the former have more or less suffered relatively for the time being. The more aggressive, the more energetic elements of the population, those who have most in the way of initiative, move to the new fields where they think the opportunity is greater. IVe have in Canada-to-day a great west that has been built up by men possessed of the necessary initiative who were content to endure all the hardships incidental to pioneering because of the future advantage they foresaw. That development in Canada has been in part from the Mari-times and has had a certain adverse effect on the Maritime provinces. But that condition is beginning more and more to right itself. It only remains for us who really desire to be helpful and not sectional or critical to seek by united action to bring about the object aimed at in this resolution, and thereby to further the larger objects which we have at heart with respect to the good of the country.	_
In conclusion may I say that during the week just past much was said in commemoration of the ninth anniversary of the great-victory at Vimy Ridge where the Canadian army corps fought as a unit, with one aim, with one idea. Speaking of that great achievement the distinguished commander of that great army corps has used the expression that at that time the nine provinces of Canada had gone up the hill side by side animated and united by a common idea and a common ideal. If that was the inspiration; if that was the means whereby victory was achieved in a great war, to the lasting glory of this country and the empire of which it is a part, surely we in this parliament representing the nine provinces of the Dominion will not in these days of peace find it difficult to go up the hill together in the solution of whatever problems may still remain in the perfecting of confederation and the great idea and ideal of national unity it was intended to serve.

Mr. Speaker, it will not
be necessary for me to comment, at least in any adverse way, on a considerable portion of the speech just delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I make this comment to concentrate attention on the lino I propose to follow more than for any other purpose: that the speech was replete with very much interesting matter, some good declamation, full of very good ideals, but was singularly wanting in discussion of what really is before the House, namely, the need, the reason for and the office of this new royal commission.
As to the resolution which we are asked to support, moved by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), I am in accord with the views expressed by the Prime Minister. The resolution certainly could not be voted against, nor do I think the resolution is in danger of misinterpretation, certainly not intentional misinterpretation, at the hands of any hon. member on this side or any side of the House. So that so far as the vote thereon is concerned, further discussion is unnecessary. The only object which can be served is to disclose what has been the course of parliament, and especially this parliament, in relation to the whole question; what has been the conduct of the administration; what now is the administration offering, and should the House be satisfied with what the government proposes.
That the responsibility is a serious one we all admit. That the problem is a complex one we equally agree. What it is we are pretty well agreed on too. This country since 1921 has suffered from very general depression. We revolved into it along wdth all other nations on this continent. We have remained! in it longer than any other nation. We-suffer from it still. Certain portions of the country have undergone greater trials than others. Those which labour under what one might describe as geographical disabilities naturally suffer the most. One of those portions is the Maritime provinces of Canada. That they have undergone many hardships in the last five years there can be no question. They were generally prosperous for a number of years before, but they recently have lost in population; they have lost in business enterprises and they have lost in hope-more so, undoubtedly, than any other portion of our country. There may be some discussion in regard to what the reason has been, but there can be no dispute as to the fact itself. These things have given rise to questioning as to whether or not they have received what was their due at the hands of the country,

speechtext:
I will broaden my remarks accordingly; I was intending to anyway, and in fact I had already done so. We know what the concomitant speeches were. There is nothing unknown. Indeed there is nothing left for investigation. If any of us had forgotten, they have certainly been brought to our minds most pointedly and forcibly by hon. members from the Maritimes this session. There may be a question as to the implications. There is no question as to the meaning of the terms, but as to the implications there may be some. But surely we in this House can judge of the implications a3 well as any living beings. We Canadian citizens here, elected to legislate for Canada, can decide what the implications are and act accordingly, we do not need any commission, however learned, to instruct us. I think there are implications beyond the exact effect of the words. For example, when in order to induce Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to enter confederation, we agreed that the Intercolonial railway would be built, it is too narrow to reason from those words that our obligation was fulfilled when the road was built. That, I presume, would be a mathematical deduction from the words; but surely it cannot be taken to be a complete deduction, because we being in control, the majority being west of the Maritimes, could build the road and then establish freight rates so high that the road would be worthless. This would not be carrying out the terms of confederation; it would be only mocking them by a subterfuge. It seems to me to follow as a necessary implication that in addition to the construction of the road we must see that it is so operated as to fulfil the well-understood purposes of its construction.
We all know what the well-understood purposes were, and therefore we know the implications. What i3 there to inquire into in order to enable us to determine what the high line of policy should be? Do we say that we do

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
not know whether they are being violated? We know what we are doing. We are doing it even ourselves; we are running the railway. We know all that. There is no fact in this sphere that is obscure; there is nothing here for a commission. We who made the contract are doing this. Do we need Sir Andrew Duncan to tell us whether we are keeping the spirit of it? We certainly do not. There is no purpose, therefore, to be found for a commission from any exploration in that field. What then i3 the commission for? Has anybody in this debate suggested up to this time what it is appointed for?
I come now to the terms of this order in council which is indeed a fearful and wonder-full production. I read the portions which intimate the several subjects into which the commission must inquire. The order recites that representations have been made and then it states:
Such representations relate more particularly to the alleged failure to use Canadian ports for Canadian trade to the extent to which they might be utilized.
That is one subject.
And to the handicaps said to result from the operation of the schedules of rates chargeable for the carriage of goods on the railways uniting the Maritime provinces with the other provinces of Canada.
Subject No. 1 is "use of ports". Subject No. 2 is "railway rates". What is the third?
And to the manner of administering that part of the Canadian National railways system which was formerly known as the Intercolonial railway-
I presume that is the work of the National railway board. I do not know whether any importance is attached to that or not. I cannot see what it is if there is any. The next is:
-by methods and conditions alleged to be inconsistent with the pledges given at the time of confederation in regard thereto and with the practice followed from the time of the construction of the railway until December, 1918.
That is all one subject-"administration of the railways." Next:
These representations have also been directed to the effects of the customs, immigration and other economic policies adopted by successive governments, of certain financial measures, and of the disposition or allotment to provinces of public lands of Canada.
I will ask the House to analyze those quotations carefully. The first is "use of ports;" the second, "rates"; the third, "administration by the government's directorate", and the fourth "the effects of the customs." The House will note how skilfully "customs" is used instead of "tariff." In a word, and to call a spade a spade, this means to inquire into tariff policy. What the "other financial measures" are I do not know, but the fourth
subject is "tariff policy." I have already read the fifth:
The disposition or allotment to provinces of public lands of Canada.
There I have reviewed the five subjects of inquiry. Let me now proceed to ask the House whether there is anything that can be described as common sense in the appointment of a commission at this hour to inquire into those subjects with a view to determination of policy. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I say that if the government would take any one of them and say: Here is a case that demands a remedy and we move to remedy it along this line, there might be reason for an inquiry to find out just what the effect of the adoption of that line of policy is, how far you should go, where it should apply, in a word, to work out the application. I do not know that there would be such reason; it would not appear to me likely, but there might be. But before you do that, to ask a commission, for example, to say what are the rights of the Maritimes in respect of those western lands,- can you think of anything more absurd? Think of asking Sir Andrew Duncan, Judge Wallace and Professor Macmillan to tell the Commons of Canada what are the rights of the Maritimes in respect of' the subject of the natural resources of Alberta 1 I put that seriously to hon. gentlemen opposite. Does their imagination enable them to think of anything more absurd? What is the limitation on this government that it cannot decide such a thing? Where is the restraint? What light is it that they are asking for? Where is it to come from? Is there anything concealed? Why, the documents have been before us for fifty years. The. only conclusion I can come to- and I submit it to the House-is that it is just a method of enabling the government not to decide for a while yet. Is that not all?
Let us come to the other points. Sir Andrew Duncan, Judge Wallace and Professor Macmillan are to help this House decide what is the best tariff policy for the Maritimes! Mr. Speaker, if you were not in the Chair you could not sit with sober mien when I put that question. This government declared, just two years ago, that so far as coal was concerned they knew what the right policy was, that it was protection and more protection. How is it that they know what the right policy is as to coal, but they do not know what it is as regards steel? How is it that they know what the right policy is for the rest of the country, but for the life of them they cannot tell what it is for the Maritimes without the help of Sir Andrew Duncan?

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
The performance of the Prime Minister . (Mr. Mackenzie King) was a pretty skilful one and I like to see a skilful performance even in a bad cause. Looking to his Progressive friends he said, and of course with an eye to Maritime sympathy:	"Do you
not remember how I appealed pathetically to you two years ago to support those extra duties on coal?" Even in the face of our declared policy we knew there would have to be an exception as regards coal, the exception as he described it, which proved the rule. He said it was a special case, forgetting for the time being that "the tariff was a tax." Has that immortal truth been lost to memory? Why was he not reminded by his Saskatchewan supporters that the tariff was a tax and that you can never in the world help an industry by taxing it? Why did they not think of that? It is quite true that two years ago the Prime Minister, commanded to do so by the Liberal party of the Maritime provinces, came to this House and demanded a higher duty on coal, and he did so in the face of a policy pronounced at the time of lower tariff on the implements of production. I wonder if coal is not an instrument of production? I appeal to the Liberal members from Saskatchewan; I appeal to those on my left, who supported a higher duty on coal at the instance of the government of the day; is not coal, of all things, an instrument of production of nearly everything? Is there anything more distinctly and fundamentally an instrument of production than coal? Then how is that to be the exception which proves the rule? Yes, they knew that there had to be more projection on coal but what else do they want -Sir Andrew Duncan to tell them. No, they >do not; they do not want Sir Andrew Duncan 4o tell them anything. This is just another stall on the tariff.
But, Mr. Speaker, what about this new tariff commission? Where has it been relegated to? That commission, with the Right Hon. George P. Graham as its head; with Mr. Daoust scattered to the four winds because he believed in protection on coal and said so, and protection all around-where is that commission now? Is it only competent to decide tariff matters for the rest of the country, and incompetent to decide them for the Maritime provinces? WThat a position the government is in! They have referred to a new commission, not ten days after their tariff commission is appointed, the question of deciding what is the right tar'ff policy for the Maritime provinces.

Let us now go back to the first, ones; what were they? To inquire into this long standing question of the use of Canadian ports a brand new commission has now been appointed which is to report to the government. The Prime Minister says, "On this we have a policy," and what is the policy? It is to use Canadian ports to the fullest possible extent. When was Canada without that policy? There never was a time when any government did not profess it, but everyone knows that the question must be reduced to the concrete, "What are you going to do to bring it about?" What is their policy on that? Their policy is nothing; objective alone is not policy: there must be a method -a plan. What is the government method- a royal commission? No, it is not one royal commission, it is two or three or four of them. Possibly I cannot account for four, but I am sure that I can recite three references of this same question to commissions. The Prime Minister read, when on his feet, a reference of the same subject to another commission, and the railway commission is engaged this very day in labouring over that very point. While the railway commission is in the throes of its toil another commission is appointed to inquire into the very same thing.
The same words apply to the subject of rates, and with that subject I have covered all. The second thing this commission is to inquire into is rates as between the Maritime provinces and the rest of the country. That was referred to the commission, but do you know, Mr. Speaker, that it was the third reference of this question? I will read the second now. I have in my hand an order in council dated June 5, 1925; it is a long order in council, but I will read the last paragraph:
The committee therefore advise that the board-
That is, the railway commission.
-be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structures of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the Dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries and in particular to:
(a)	The claim asserted on behalf of the Maritime provinces that they are entitled to the restoration of the rate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919;
(b)	The encouragement of the movement of traffic through Canadian ports;
(c)	The increased traffic westward and eastward through Pacific coast ports owing to the expansion of trade with the Orient and to the transportation of products through the Panama canal.

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
So this is the third reference to a commission, but that is not all. These things have been before the railway commission ever since the commission was\ created 1 Ever since that commission became a commission its plain duty under the Railway Act was tc erect a rate structure based on these very principles. So if reference to a commission would cure this situation the government has tried the application of that dose in repeated and unstinted measure. Month after month they come before parliament; now it is referred to this commission and again to that commission. But can you imagine the chaos we ai'e in now, with the railway commission sitting on these very questions, hearing evidence and arguments; and in the midst of it all there is another commission appointed, headed by Sir Andrew Duncan, to make a thorough inquiry, over top of all the others, into the very same thing.
This is the government policy, and we are asked to believe that it is devised because of anxiety for unity in Canada. Commissions to make unity 1 After this commission comes back *where will we be? I will make a prophecy; we will have another commission appointed to inquire into the same subject again. If this agitation keeps up, a few months more will see a reference of this same subject to some other commission; that is the "fixed" policy of the government.
It does seem clear that until there is an announcement of a step to be taken, something concrete and definite, there is no purpose which this commission can serve.' However good the commission may be, however well intentioned its members, what purpose can the imagination of man divine which this commission may serve at this time? If there is something in the way of inquiry as to the assessment or effect of its policy or as to its application, that is one thing. But to appoint a commission to devise a policy, and especially to appoint such a commission after there had been repeated directions to another commission over and over again is to me the very acme of the absurd.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) spoke this afternoon. I do not yet very well know what his views are. He was very timid about pronouncing himself, but he did say that he had been opposed all along to the acquirement of the Canadian Northern railway and subsequently to the acquirement of the Grand Trunk railway; and in that way he sought to wash his hands of the present situation. "I am not responsible" he said, "I fought the acquirement of the Canadian Northern away back in 1914, I also fought
the acquirement of the Grand Trunk in 1919. May I ask any member of this House: Does the present situation flow from the acquirement of the Canadian Northern railway, or the acquirement of the Grand Trunk railway; does any single atom of it flow from such a source? The minister of National Defence suggested one thing-he did not say it [DOT]-he suggested-I do not think anyone else would seriously suggest it-that because in acquiring the Grand Trunk we got the line which runs to Portland, there flows from this fact the greater use of that port. Can anybody follow his reasoning? Because we own the stock of the Grand Trunk instead of the old Grand Trunk shareholders owning it, does that fact cause more railway freight to run to Portland? Well, if so, who is responsible? Is it not the directorate appointed by this government? Because we own that line to the terminus with the other lines, if there is *ny result in the world, it gives us more commanding control of the situation. Let me repeat. If the fact of our ownership of the Portland line affects the situation in any way whatever, it affects it to give the government of the day a greater control of the direction of traffic.
I know there was a motion moved, and I wondered that the minister of Defence read it -I noticed he did not read it very loudly -a motion moved by the Minister of Justice, then the member for Kamouraska, in amendment to the motion for the third reading of the Grand Trunk bill of 1919. I think I have it here.

Well, I certainly compliment them that their second thought is better than their first, for they all supported it, every one of them. That they are ashamed of it now is a tribute to their intelligence today, if not to their judgment then. It was referred to by the Minister of National Defence: I had almost forgotten it. He referred to it by way of emphasizing the consistent stand taken by the Liberal party on this question. "Why" he said, "there was moved a motion that we do not read that Grand Trunk bill a third time." But why? "Because by acquiring railways in the States we would land ourselves in international complications-complications so serious that they

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
would drift us into annexation." The House really will hardly believe that any hon. member could have moved such a resolution. Only in 1919-I remember the debate well- over and over again we were warned that if we got the stock of the Grand Trunk instead of the stockholders in England owning it, then, as the Grand Trunk included some lines in the States, that would land us into trouble with Washington. All sorts of international complications would ensue, and we would be in danger of annexation. Mr. Speaker, it was really for that the Liberal party voted! Well, we have had the road now for seven years, and who has ever heard of any international complications? I appeal to the memories of members of the Liberal party. The member for Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier) shakes his head in the negative. He is the first one to record himself honestly. There has never been the slightest sign or symptom of any such complications. But that was the objection taken to the acquirement. So far as affecting this problem is concerned, if it had any effect at all, it gave the government greater control over the situation.
Then the Minister of National Defence said, " I opposed the acquirement even of the Canadian Northern." What relation that point has to the question I at least am at a loss to divine. He said, " Why, I fought against it in 1914, even though at that time we were only guaranteeing the bonds of the railway." The Minister of National Defence did oppose the guarantee of the bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway in 1914. He opposed it all the way through. We felt we had to guarantee them or have the system go into liquidation, which in the end would cost us far more. But did he oppose it because it was a step towards the acquirement of the road? Will the House believe me when I state that he opposed it because we were not inserting in the guarantee agreement a clause to provide for the acquirement of the road? I have before me a motion made by- I hope nobody will deny its authorship-made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It will be found in Hansard of June 2, 1914, at page 4634:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved, seconded by Mr. Pugsley, that the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be resolved that under existing circumstances no assistance should be given to the 'Canadian Northern Railway Company unless at the same time it is provided that the government have power, within a reasonable time, to acquire ownership of the entire stock of the company at a price to be fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed $30,000,000.
If hon. members will turn to page 4633 of the same Hansard they will find among those

voting " yea " on that amendment the name of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysbor-ough (Mr. Macdonald).

speechtext: How did the member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) vote on that occasion?

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
The member for West Calgary is not down as voting at all, but if he had voted in favour of acquiring the railway he would not be standing on his feet to-day and boasting that he had always opposed its acquirement. It was not therefore the acquirement of the road that the Minister of National Defence voted against. He voted against our assisting it without enabling the country to acquire it. He wanted us then and there to take steps to acquire it. And he was ready to pay $30,000,000 for the capital stock. So hon. members will seee just how much sincerity there has been in this campaign and talk about the Liberal party having been against the acquirement of the National railways. They were against it just because we found it necessary to acquire those railways, and up to the time when we found that it was essential, that we could not help 12 m. it, they were urging us on in that very direction, finding fault with us and voting for amendments because we would not proceed with the acquirement rapidly enough.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the history of the acquirement question. Again I say, it has nothing in the world to do with this situation. This is a question of rates. The subject of rates is just as much under our control to-day, even more under our control now that we are the owners of one great portion of Canadian roads, than if we were owners of none. It would be, it is true, under our control in any event, even were we not owners. But the question before us is this: How can we so exercise our control as to give the assistance necessary to meet this situation to the far off extremes of our country? I have taken the pains and taken the responsibility, and met with very considerable antagonism on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, in an effort to outline one method which could be adopted to meet the Maritime situation on the side of transportation. It was announced in a resolution moved on the 2nd of June last. By that resolution I still adhere, and by that resolution I believe every member of this House on this side adheres. Our criticism, therefore, is not wholly destructive. We are on record in constructive fashion. Where are the government? We are now almost a year past that date, and their policy

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
is " royal commissions " still. Let the government suggest some other line upon which we can move. What did they say when this line was suggested? I appeal to the Maritime members on whose behalf they are so sympathetic now. They stood up in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec and said: Meighen wants to take out of the treasury of Canada a share of the freight rate to enable Maritime goods to get to these central provinces.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext: The Tories said it.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS AND UNDERSTANDINGS RESPECTING FREIGHT TRAFFIC AND RATES
speechtext:
Yes, and we were denounced for making that proposal. It was declared to be unfair to the central provinces of Canada; it was declared to be unfair to those producing goods in the central provinces to have to sell against the Maritimes, who were to ship them at rates assisted by parliament. These were the men who now stand up and appeal to our Atlantic brothers to believe that they are at great pains and agonies because of the troubles of the Maritimes. If there is any better way than my suggestion we would all like to hear it. I know' of no better way myself. If a better can be found, I will follow it. But I proposed that just described, and I venture to suggest that the government will come to it before long themselves.
I was not going to mention again the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), but now that he is in, I think I ^should. There was read this afternoon by the hon. senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) an inquiry put to the Minister of National Defence before the 1921 election. The minister will remember that the 1921 election was run by the Liberal party on the cry: "Take the Intercolonial out of the National system; put it back where it was," and the Minister of National Defence, of course, was the most vociferous and authoritative voice behind the cry. This question was put to him during the 1921 compaign:
Realizing the importance of the campaign which our newspaper has consistently supported for restoration of Maritime rights with Canadian National Railway by establishment of eastern unit, with headquarters at Moncton in charge of Maritime trained men, we would appreciate if you would favour us with a brief definite statement of your attitude on the question.
Here ia the answer:
For the past year and a half I have consistently urged that the only method to enable the industries of the Maritime provinces to be carried on with any degree of success would be by detaching the Intercolonial altogether from the Canadian National railway and Grand Trunk railway connections, and running and operating it as it was operated for forty years under the terms of confederation.
One thing I will say about that declaration:
It is clear, it is definite, there is no misunderstanding it at all. He goes on:
We would thus be freed from the taxation which is now imposed upon the patrons of the road for the purpose of paying the interest upon the enormous debts contracted by the Canadian National Railway in its construction in western Canada. The control of Ihe Intercolonial must be taken from Toronto and vested in Moncton, where it always was, and the railway should be officered by men in sympathy with Maritime interests and Maritime rights.
Now when faced with this to-day and questioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), what was the statement made by the Minister of National Defence? " Why, certainly," he said, "I was against the Intercolonial being run in 1922 by "-I do not know just how he put it; I wish he would put it just the same way again, but this was the effect of it: " Because I opposed the taking over of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk, therefore I was consistent in 1921 when I made that statement to the Halifax Herald." What has the opposing of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk to do with that statement? That statement was made two years after they were both our property. Nor did the minister refer to his opposition because specifically he referred to a year and a half before the time he sent his message to the Herald. He says: " For ' a year and a half' I have been urging the taking of the Intercolonial out of the National system altogether, and putting it back where it w'as and where it had been for forty years." But did he do it when he got into power? Did he take a single step towards taking it out? Certainly he did not. I will not say he never intended to; I do not know, but he ought to admit to the House that he was wholly wrong in 1921, and that the votes he got on that declaration he had no right to whatever. All the votes obtained through the Maritime provinces, obtained by proclamations to take the Intercolonial out of the National system, all these votes were fraudulently obtained. The Minister of National Defence sat four years in this House before he went back to his people, and never in all that time had he taken a single step towards redeeming the pledge he openly and publicly gave in the fall of 1921.
The Intercolonial is part of the National system There is an Atlantic division at Moncton. There could not have been one established until the Grand Trunk was fully amalgamated. That could not take place, did not take place even under this government until the end of 1922 or the beginning of 1923. We could not possibly do so for the reason that the arbitration proceedings had

Maritime Rights-Mr. Meighen
not been fully completed and executed. But I stated in that campaign that when such amalgamation was done there would be one established, that the directorate had so pronounced, that its headquarters would be in the Maritime provinces, and that its jurisdiction would extend westward as far as the end of 'the Intercolonial. Such was the purpose of the government of that day. And in opposition to that expressed declaration of policy, the Minister of National Defence and his followers in the Maritime provinces stumped those provinces and declared that if they were elected they would take the Intercolonial out of the National system and restore it to the place where it had been for forty years, and run it as a distinct and separate entity. There is the breach of faith on the part of the Liberal party of this country. It is because of such things that disaffection exists to-day.
I stood in this House some weeks ago and said, as I have always done, that I did not believe the taking of the Intercolonial out would itself be any remedy to the Maritime provinces. It is not whether the National Railway board runs it or not that counts; it is the rates that count; it is the burden on the people who ship goods; that is what tells in the success or failure of trade along its line. So I think I have brought home to the Minister of National Defence conduct which certainly did not help him in the late campaign, and which no doubt was partly explanatory of his flight from Pictou into the county of Antigonish-Guysborough.
_ Now let me say, Mr. Speaker, that in my judgment this problem of Maritime rights mainly is a question, first and foremost, of transportation, and secondly, of tariff adjustments. I am advised-I may not be advised correctly-that a representative of the National Railway board, speaking before the railway commission recently, made the statement that the Intercolonial was not built to give the Maritimes access to the central provinces; but rather was built to give the production of the central provinces access to the Maritimes. I know the gentleman to whom those words are ascribed, and I find it hard to think he would make such a statement, but if he did, I feel he has wholly misapprehended the central purpose which dictated the construction of the road. The road undoubtedly was constructed by way of concession to the Maritimes, and to enable those provinces to reach the central markets of our country. That it was hoped it would serve the complementary purpose there is no doubt, but to intimate that the complementary purpose, access to the Maritimes from the central prov-
inces, was the primary objective of its construction is wholly to misread history and to misconstrue facts. To serve the Maritimes wa3 the great purpose of the Intercolonial, and in national policy to-day this must be taken into account. In deciding what we are going to do to meet the special transportation difficulties of these provinces we must keep ever before us the primary and essential end for which the Intercolonial was built. Along that line you can give relief. My method of acting along that line I have indicated to this House and the country; I call upon the government to indicate theirs. I say to them: do not hide behind more royal commissions. Do not trifle with public opinion any longer. Do not waste the country's money. Do not do what is far worse-waste the country's time and test the patience of our people by those devious, scientific procrastinations.
And then as to the tariff. The tariff has been manipulated in late years undoubtedly to the disadvantage of the Maritime provinces. I wonder by what colour of right the tariff on steel, for example, is taken, the protection cast away and the industry virtually paralyzed in order that some pet hobby about men specially engaged in making "implements of production" being entitled to a singular line of treatment may be carried into effect. All this has hurt the Maritimes. In reference to the tariff the line which must be taken is this: Remove the disabilities that have been placed uipon those provinces of late years and turn our tariff policy in the direction of developing industries in the Maritime provinces by giving those industries protection. I am advised that in the late campaign as the discussion reached its climax and election day approached down in Cape Breton island-yes, and in territory near Cape Breton island as well,-every Liberal candidate was compelled to come out and declare that he supported the principle of protection for Maritime products. I ask that this fact sink into the minds of hon. members from Saskatchewan. "Oh," we are told by the Prime Minister, "if we only had that reciprocity treaty!" Did you ever hear anything discussed in this House and the government utterly at a loss for an excuse that they did not bring up the reciprocity pact? The members from the Maritime provinces as well as from the west will not forget that only a few weeks ago I challenged the government face to face on that issue. I challenged any one of them to stand up and say that if he could re-enact the provisions of that treaty to-day he would do so. Not one of them responded. It is a great treaty as long

Business of the House
as it it out of existence; it is a great treaty as long as it is not readvanced; but I invite them now just to reintroduce that treaty and let us go to the country upon it. The Prime Minister says, "Oh, if we had reciprocity in natural products!" Did you observe this prayer was offered up just about two paragraphs after he had stated that we needed higher protection on coal? Did you observe anything in the reciprocity pact of 1911 for free trade in coal? Mention was made there about free fruit and about free vegetables, but not about free coal. I wonder is coal not a natural product? What is unnatural about it? What is to be thought, then, of the professed fidelity of hon. gentlemen opposite towards free trade or reciprocity in natural products? The only consistent fixed policy of the government is royal commissions. Against that policy I appeal and I ask the government first to lay out the path along which they intend to travel; I ask them to tell us something they intend to do, tell us the policy they intend to adopt. Having done that they will have discharged their duty, and the country at least will have respect for them as men of courage and men who understand their responsibilities.
